###### **COMPARISON OF VARIOUS METHODS FOR CALCULATING CASH COSTS - FOCUS ON NICKEL INDUSTRY** 

By 

Peter Jolly 

Highlands Pacific Ltd, Australia 

Presenter and Corresponding Author 

**Peter Jolly** pjolly@highlandspacific.com 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

This paper has been prepared to help clarify the term “cash costs” and “unit cash costs (costs on a per mass basis)” which often appears in material associated with developing and promoting investment in mining ventures and mineral commodities. 

In a strict accounting sense the term cash costs has a specific meaning as it refers to the cost of transactions when using cash, credit or cheques. This paper is not referring to this definition or subject. 

In the mining industry, in an effort to quantify the costs associated with a mining venture, the term unit cash costs (often simply stated as the cash costs) are often cited as one of the indices to monitor and rank a specific venture’s performance against others. To be able to accurately carry out such an analysis requires a uniform approach and lots of data both from the producers and the smelters and refineries who take all play a part in transforming a mineral in the ground to a form that is useful to an end user

, such as stainless steel producer, nickel plater, alloy manufacturer as is the case when referring to nickel. 

The paper has a focus on the nickel industry although should apply to other industries such as the copper, lead and zinc. The paper is not concerned with comparing one operation against another, rather it outlines and discusses the methods used to make this comparison. It is arguable that the nickel industry brings complications compared to say the copper industry, in that there are a variety of “finished products”, such as FeNi, nickel salts and pure nickel metal. 

As highlighted in this paper there are no standard internationally agreed methods used to calculate a cash cost curve, so care must be taken to examine the underlying assumptions when comparing cost curves. 

While the author originally set out to make a case for greater standardization in defining the term cash costs and the associated cash cost curves, the author is now of the opinion that this may not be possible due to the sensitivity of reporting commercial terms. 

There is no doubt that the use of the term cash costs will endure as it has become an often used measure of company operating performance as well as for analysts comparing industry trends. 

2 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

This paper has been prepared to help clarify the term “cash costs” and “unit cash costs (costs on a per mass basis)” which often appears in material associated with developing and promoting investment in mining ventures and mineral commodities. 

In a strict accounting sense the term cash costs has a specific meaning as it refers to the cost of transactions when using cash, credit or cheques. This paper is not referring to this definition or subject. 

In the mining industry, in an effort to quantify the costs associated with a mining venture, the term unit cash costs (often simply stated as the cash costs) are often cited as one of the indices to monitor and rank a specific venture’s performance against others. To be able to accurately carry out such an analysis requires a uniform approach and lots of data both from the producers and the smelters and refineries who take all play a part in transforming a mineral in the ground to a form that is useful to an end user, such as stainless steel producer, nickel plater, alloy manufacturer as is the case when referring to nickel. 

In an effort to clarify the methods and approach used the author has contacted Minecost<sup>(1)</sup> , Wood Mackenzie<sup>(2)</sup> and AME<sup>(3)</sup> , all international companies that offer services that enable investors and interested parties to compare cash costs across an industry. The author acknowledges their contribution and takes all responsibility for any errors of interpretation that may have occurred during the communications. If time had of permitted the author would have also contacted CRU, another international organization offering services in this area, to gain their input and perspective as well.

The paper has a focus on the nickel industry although should apply to other industries such as the copper, lead and zinc. The paper is not concerned with comparing one operation against another, rather it outlines and discusses the methods used to make this comparison. It is arguable that the nickel industry brings complications compared to say the copper industry, in that there are a variety of “finished products”, such as FeNi, nickel salts and pure nickel metal. Figure 1 shows the actual and forecast production of nickel by process, courtesy of Wood Mackenzie(4) . 3 **Figure 1: Nickel Production by Process****(4)** Figure 2 shows the actual and forecast production of nickel from sulphides and laterites, again courtesy of Wood Mackenzie(4) . Figures 1 and 2 show the trends away from sulphides to laterites and also the increasing production of nickel from FeNi and HPAL operations. As more investment is made into these technologies, investors will have an interest in comparing the costs of various operations. The cash cost curve is one way of ranking and comparing these investments. **Figure 2: Comparison of Nickel Production from Laterites and Sulphides****(4)** The author believes that there is a need for greater standardization of the methods used to calculate cash costs, which would improve investors and observers understanding of the industry. However, it needs to be acknowledged that many operations do not publish all of the data necessary to quantify the cash costs, as some of this data, such as the sales and marketing terms, are confidential. This is where organizations, such as Minecost and the like, can serve a useful 4 function by collecting and analysing this information and publishing in a standard form (for a price) that retains confidentiality. ###### **BACKGROUND - REPORTING OF CASH COSTS AND THE CASH COST CURVE** It has been the authors’ experience that companies often report their quarterly or annual cash costs on a per unit basis. Murrin Murrin (laterite) and Mincor (sulphide) are good examples. The Table 1 below, taken from the Murrin Murrin quarterly reports posted on the company’s website are an example. All footnotes to the table are reported in full to show how the cash costs (in this case C11 cash costs) are reported and used to stress company performance. It should be noted that the costs are often quoted on a unit **_payable_** nickel basis rather than a **_contained_** nickel basis – this can lead to confusion when making comparisons with others who use a different basis. This point will be discussed in full later in the paper. In addition to companies using the concept of cash costs to keep track of their performance investors often want to compare performance of one operation to another or for that matter examine trends across the whole industry. As mentioned previously, there are several organizations offering such analyses. AME<sup>(3)</sup> has kindly made available the curve below (Figure 4), which compares the costs of various sulphide operations to those of laterite operations (2012 data). To retain confidentiality, names of the various operations have been removed. Some features of this curve are as follows; 

1. The unit cash costs (x axis) in this case are US$/lb nickel payable. US$ are always used when preparing costs curves, so exchange rates become very important when collecting and comparing costs across different countries. 

2. The reason that some operations show a negative cash cost is because of the by-product credits, which can be substantial. This is the usual case for Norilsk sulphide operations in Russia. 

3. The horizontal axis shows the cumulative payable nickel in a given year. This is not the total metal delivered to the market as payable nickel is a subset of this larger figure. The graph has been truncated to show production with cash costs less than 10US$/lb payable nickel. 

4. All operations below the LME nickel price line are typically profitable although financing costs of the operation are not included in this definition of cash costs so definitive conclusions on profitability cannot be deduced from such curves. 

5. This cost curve is **_not as strongly dependent_** on the price of nickel (for a fixed unit refining costs) allowing the unit profit margin to be read directly off the curve (see sections 3.1 and 3.2). It should be noted for cost curves developed by others this is not always the case, as will be discussed later in the analysis section. 

6. It would be possible to construct many variations on this curve, which may include a comparison of HPAL laterite operations to heap leach for example.

The following section outlines rigorous definition(s) of the cash cost curve so that an analysis can performed to understand some of the differences between the various methods used. It should be noted that there may be other definitions of cash cost other than those defined in this paper. Needless to say it would be good to have one agreed industry standard! ###### **DEFINITION OF CASH COSTS** When going through what little literature that exists on the subject it seems that the Gold Institute(5) were the first to try and formalize a definition of cash costs and this is often referred to in the literature and company brochures. However, there are no IFRS or GAAP binding requirements that require companies to report their cash costs in a standard way. This seems to be the case across all commodity types. Smith **_et al_****_(_**6) (formerly Brook Hunt) has published definitions pertaining to the calculation of cash costs and has formulated the concepts of C1, C2 and C3 cash costs. The complete elaboration of the definition of these terms is outside the scope of this paper. However, the term C1 is equivalent to the definition of one of the cash costs defined in this paper, namely “Method 2” (refer to Tables and graphs throughout the paper). In effort to clarify differences between the various approaches data from a “hypothetical mine” mine is used. The operation is a laterite mine that produces an intermediate product for sale to a refinery that makes nickel and cobalt (a by-product) as finished products (see Figure 6). Of course there are many variations of this production model, such as the production of FeNi, in-house production of pure metal such as occurs at Murrin Murrin and the shipment of laterites ores to smelters or refiners to mention just a few. It is also possible to define a cash cost from a **_company perspective_** , defined as follows;

Cash Cost ($) **=** Mining cost 

**+** Plant (in-house refining) **+** G&A (General and Administration) **+** Royalty costs **+** Shipping costs ……………………………………………………… (8) 

This equation simply defines the cost of producing material prior to refining and receiving credits. It would be a useful KPI for a miner to track internal operating cash costs (see Figure 3). 

To arrive at the cash costs, on a unit mass basis, it is necessary to divide equation 1 (and 8) by a suitable divisor, which is now discussed. 

###### **INFLUENCE OF THE DENOMINATOR ON UNIT CASH COSTS** 

As has been mentioned that units cash costs can be expressed in several ways and careful attention needs to be made when reading or reviewing figures to understand the precise definition used. One of the key differences between the various methods is the denominator used in the calculation of unit cash costs. The issue is discussed in the 2006 paper by Smith **_et al_**<sup>**_(_**6)</sup> . Possible divisors include **_contained_** , **_recovered_** or **_paid (or payable)_** metal. 

The **recovered metal** basis can be an appropriate method to use when totalling the cost of each processing stage (mine, processing, smelter and refinery), in order to determine the total costs of the metal reaching the market place, i.e., the industry cost of production. Wood Mackenzie often use this method in their publications<sup>(4)</sup> and larger producers such as Xstrata<sup>(8)</sup> use the method to show investors their favourable position of the industry cash cost curve. 

Another option is to use **paid metal** as the divisor. This method seems to be favoured by Australian companies reporting their quarterly and annual results (see Tables 1 and 2). It reflects the arms length contract terms between the mining operation and the smelter/refinery taking the off-take. 

A unit “profit margin” can then be defined as; 

Profit Margin ($/Mass) = LME price nickel – Cash Cost /Mass  ………………… (9) 

Where, the “Mass” divisor is either **_recovered metal_** (method 2) or **_paid metal_** (method 1). 

###### **INFLUENCE OF A FIXED REFINING COST ON UNIT CASH COSTS** 

By examining equations 1 and 2, it can be noted that that the unit cash costs are largely independent of the nickel

price **IF** the refinery costs are not a direct function of the LME price. This is the case for integrated producers and independents that do not have strong price participation terms with refineries (such as is the case for method 1). 

Figure 7 has been prepared to graphically demonstrate this point. The figure was generated using the base data in Table 4 and then varying the nickel price while holding all other parameters constant.

The slight positive slope of the line (method 1) is due to the weak dependence on the royalty costs, which are small relative to other costs. This independence has implications when using the cash cost curve to estimate a company’s profitability (section 4.2).

They are purely fictitious numbers although might be considered typical in an HPAL operation making an intermediate product. However, each HPAL operation has its own operational peculiarities. For example, factors such as the ore body type, the purchasing or manufacturing arrangements for acid (a key cost in HPAL leaching operations) and the cost of power, are key determining factors in arriving at the cost of production. Similarly the refining costs (and hence charges) are also driven by operating costs such as energy, labour, consumables, maintenance etc.

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The following conclusions and observations are made; 

1. **_Payable_** method (Method 1) seems to be popular in Australia for reporting company performance. Cash costs derived using this method are generally higher than those derived on a **_recovered_** nickel basis (Method 2) 

2. There is no doubt that a cost curve (either on a **_recovered_** nickel basis or a **_payable_** basis) allows an operation to ranked amongst others in the industry or a sub section of the industry, such as HPAL operators. 

3. In order to be able to develop an industry cost curve a lot of information is required, including marketing terms, shipping costs, recoveries, refining costs and company costs of production. Mostly this information is not available in the public domain. Organizations such as AME, Minecost, CRU and Wood Mackenzie offer paid services to provide costs curves while retaining client confidentiality. 

4. After detailed discussions with AME<sup>(3)</sup> it is apparent that since 2007 the degree of price participation that refineries once enjoyed is very much diminished, leading to a less LME price dependent refining change. AME apply economic concepts of fixed and variable asset specific costs in the production of their cost curve and they are perhaps unique in their approach. 

5. It is the author’s belief that the cost curve, relative to the prevailing metal price curve, is only a rough guide to a company’s profitability as many costs terms are left out. It’s quite possible that a mining operation may have a mid tier cash cost but be unprofitable. 

6. Concerning the nickel industry, it needs to be noted that there are many variations in final product, unlike say the copper industry, where essentially pure copper is the final product. As often stated up to 60% of all nickel ends up in stainless steels and the majority of this would **_not_** come from pure cathode nickel. Given th

is situation one wonders the merit in using a cash cost curve to compare one finished form of nickel against another such as, for example, an operation producing FeNi to an operation producing pure nickel cathode. Of course comparing operations 

18 

producing the same end products does make a lot of sense, at least for benchmarking purposes and for promoting an investment strategy. 

As highlighted in this paper there are no standard internationally agreed methods used to calculate a cash cost curve, so care must be taken to examine the underlying assumptions when comparing cost curves. 

While the author originally set out to make a case for greater standardization in defining the term cash costs and the associated cash cost curves, he is now of the opinion that this may not be possible due to the sensitivity of reporting commercial terms. 

There is no doubt that the use of the term cash costs will endure as it has become an often used measure of company operating performance as well as for analysts comparing industry trends.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Recent literature reports laterite processes based on sulphate, chloride and nitrate chemistry.  This paper presents a study of the mass/energy balances associated with processing limonite and saprolite via each of these three different routes, based on information published for each route. The mass/energy balances are analyzed and the variable operating costs potentially associated with each are calculated from the reagent and utility consumptions predicted by the mass/energy balances.  The cal

culated reagent/utility costs are compared and discussed. 

20 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

About sixty percent of the world’s current nickel production comes from sulphide sources<sup>(1)</sup> , but laterite deposits account for about sixty percent of the world’s total nickel resources<sup>(2)</sup> . As world demand increases and currently exploited sulphide sources of nickel become depleted, if no major new sources of sulphide nickel appear it is inevitable that more of the world’s nickel will have to be extracted from laterite deposits. Pyrometallurgy is an established technology for producing ferronickel or nickel matte from laterite ores containing about two percent nickel or higher, 10-15 percent Mg and low iron (13-20 percent), i.e. principally the saprolite fraction of the laterite<sup>(3)</sup> . The Caron Process is another established technology that extracts nickel and cobalt from laterite, again mainly from saprolite<sup>(3)</sup> . A more recent technology is high pressure acid leaching (HPAL) in which nickel is extracted from laterite ore using sulphuric acid at high temperature and pressure, this time mainly from the higher iron lower magnesium content limonite fraction. There is no one commercial process that can treat the whole laterite orebody. 

Laterite ores originate from the weathering of ultramafic rocks (e.g. olivine and pyroxene)<sup>(4)</sup> . The more-weathered upper layer of a typical laterite profile is referred to as the limonite zone, below that is a transition zone called the nontronite or clay zone, below that is a less-weathered zone called the saprolite zone and below the saprolite zone is the un-weathered bedrock. The limonite zone contains primarily the mineral goethite or other hydrated iron oxides, containing nickel in the lattice of the iron minerals. The primary constituent of the saprolite zone is hydrated magnesium silicates with nickel and cobalt replacing some of the magnesium<sup>(4)</sup> . Saprolitic and transition laterites containing about 1.5 or more percent nickel would be considered appropriate candidates for smelting or the Caron Process. Lower grade laterites have typically been seen as candidates for hydrometallurgical processing. 

Hydrometallurgical processing of laterite begins with an acid leach of some kind. The dominant acid so far has been sulphuric acid, but work has been published on processes using hydrochloric acid or nitric acid<sup>(3,5)</sup> . Sulphuric acid, hydrochloric acid and nitric acid being the three major mineral acids, the question arose of whether or not processes using these acids have intrinsic advantages, depending on the ore treated and the acid used. This paper presents a study examining hydrometallurgical circuits in which these three acids are used to extract nickel and cobalt from laterite. Two laterite ores and two moisture levels were chosen for this study, i.e. limonite and saprolite, at 5 and 20 percent moisture. Process modelling was used to generate

mass/energy balances for each ore, for published circuits using sulphuric acid, hydrochloric acid or nitric acid.

This molten salt hydrate is heated to 500°C, causing it to decompose to solid magnesium oxide, steam and gaseous O2, NO and NO2. The NO and NO2 used in the model represent the NOx referred to in the literature published on the Direct Nickel process<sup>(8)</sup> . The NOx is converted back to nitric acid using the method patented by Drinkard<sup>(9)</sup> , in which NO reacts with HNO3 in the presence of dissolved trivalent nitrogen, then the solution is oxidized to nitric acid with air. The gas from the thermal decomposition step and the steam from the preceding evaporation step are contacted with the aqueous nitric acid scrubbed from the steam from the evaporation step after the leach, and air is added. The NOx is completely oxidized, giving aqueous nitric acid (60% HNO3) that returns to the leach and the re-dissolution step after the first precipitation step. The steam and gaseous nitric acid leaving the iron and aluminium hydrolysis stages, plus the steam, a

cid and nitrogen oxides leaving the evaporation and decomposition stages, carry latent heat that can be recycled. The atmospheric boiling point of the solution leaving the leach train is over 110°C. Injecting the steam and gaseous nitric acid from the two hydrolysis stages releases that heat of condensation at the temperature of the leach, thus it can be used to raise steam at 100°C and atmospheric pressure. The heat of reaction of the leach also contributes to the energy that can be captured as atmospheric pressure steam. The steam from the evaporation step ahead of the magnesium nitrate decomposition step, plus the steam and nitrogen oxides from the decomposition step, are cooled to 110°C in the acid regeneration stage of the process, raising more steam at 100°C and atmospheric pressure. 

The atmospheric pressure steam raised from the cooling steps described in the preceding paragraph is not shown in Figure 3. The process model uses the energy balances over those steps 

27 

to calculate the amount of steam raised, and applies it in the heat exchanger shown above the label “Energy from process” in the separate little circuit at the top left of Figure 3. The waste heat from the process is used to raise steam at atmospheric pressure from boiler feed water, then the steam is split, part being expanded through a turbine and condensed, the power from the expansion turbine driving a compressor that raises the pressure of the balance of the steam such that its saturation temperature is high enough for it to be used as a heat source in the evaporation section. The heat exchanger labelled “Energy to process” represents that. The high temperature condensate is flashed to atmospheric pressure and the steam released joins the atmospheric steam raised from the process waste heat. The two condensate streams become boiler feed water for recycle. 

The energy input to the circuit not covered by the energy recycled as condensing compressed steam is supplied from an external source. The process model assumed natural gas, heating value 55.6 MJ/kg, as the heating utility.

The chloride and nitrate circuits are not in commercial operation and are therefore new technologies, as yet unproven commercially. This exercise focuses on the mass/energy balances emanating from process models representing the sulphate, chloride and nitrate circuits, calculating the amounts of the various reagents and utilities used by each circuit and using assumed unit costs to convert those quantities into variable costs. Table 21 lists the calculated reagent/utility costs for the three circuits, for limonite and saprolite feed at the two moisture levels chosen for this study, for no energy recycle and with energy recycle, using the unit costs shown in the breakdowns for the individual circuits. The case of the modified nitrate circuit with energy recycle is also listed. The unit costs used were gathered at the end of 2011, for a Canadian location. For different specific projects, the unit cost numbers would change. Fixed operating and capital cost calculations could certainly affect the ranking of these three circuits, but that has been left out of this exercise. In the case of the laterite feed, the trade-off between the somewhat higher reagent/utility costs for the sulphate circuit may be that technical risk would be lower for that circuit. The sulphate circuit is 31 unaffected by the moisture level in the incoming limonite because the feed is adjusted to 30 percent solids ahead of the autoclave section using water recycled within the circuit, so the autoclave train, which is where energy is used, sees the same feed no matter what the moisture in the incoming laterite. Any excess water leaves as waste water. The reason for that is that the limonite consumes more acid in the leach than the saprolite does, because of the higher iron content in the limonite. The higher magnesium content of the saprolite only partially offsets the reduction in acid consumption due to its lower iron content. For the feeds selected for this exercise, the limonite consumes 916 kg of HCl per tonne of dry ore, compared to 698 kg of HCl per tonne of dry saprolite. The increased amount of iron thus requires an increased circulation of ferric chloride to the hydrolysis section and a higher circulation of acid back to the leach, plus more evaporation and condensation of water. Since the hydrolysis reactions are endothermic, the higher acid consumption in the leach, giving a higher hydrolysis duty, increases the energy consumption of the chloride circuit. The hydrolysis of magnesium requires more energy in the case of saprolite than limonite because the saprolite contains more magnesium than the limonite, but the difference is not enough to offset the effect of the higher acid consumption in the leach, for limonite relative to saprolite, in the chloride circuit. According to the process models, the energy consumption in the nitrate circuit is higher than in the chloride circuit. One reason for that would be because of the higher evaporation load in the nitrate circuit. If the nitrate circuit can be modified to not quench the hot hematite slurry and alumina slurry into water, and to wash these filter cakes using less water, the overall energy consumption of the nitrate circuit would be reduced considerably. Another reason for the higher energy consumption in the nitrate circuit, relative to the chloride circuit, is that the thermal decomposition of magnesium nitrate is more endothermic than the hydrolysis and calcination of magnesium chloride. **Figure 4 – Heats of reaction** The first graph in Figure 4 shows that the energy required to thermally decompose magnesium nitrate is substantially more than the energy required to hydrolyse magnesium chloride. The second graph shows that hydrolysis of ferric nitrate requires more energy than hydrolysis of ferric chloride. While this may be simplistic, it does begin to explain the differences between the energy balances of the nitrate and the chloride circuits. Another con

sideration in comparing the energy consumptions of the chloride and nitrate circuits is that in the nitrate circuit magnesium oxide is recycled to precipitate aluminium, nickel and cobalt. The recycled magnesium oxide reverts to magnesium nitrate and that magnesium nitrate is redecomposed to nitrogen oxides and magnesium oxide. The recycle of magnesium oxide increases the amount of magnesium nitrate decomposed, hence raising the energy demand in that part of the nitrate circuit. 

The process models calculate very low losses of chloride and nitrate from the respective circuits.  n both circuits, the losses are small amounts in the residues and products. The nitrate models predict a make-up acid of 0.03 kg of nitric acid per tonne of dry feed and the chloride models predict an acid make-up of 0.1 to 0.2 kg of HCl per tonne of dry feed. At those levels the cost of the make-up acid is trivial. However, the Direct Nickel web site<sup>(11)</sup> lists an overall consumption of 30 kg of nitric acid per tonne of ore. This is orders of magnitude greater than the make-up calculated in this exercise. If the actual make-up of nitric acid is of the order of 30 instead of 0.03 kg per tonne of ore, and assuming the nitric acid cost used in this exercise, that would raise the variable cost by about $1.1 per pound of nickel plus cobalt produced. For limonite, that would make the nitrate circuit more expensive than the sulphate circuit. A crucial part of the nitrate circuit, therefore, is the acid regeneration stage. An overall make-up of 30 kg of HNO₃ per tonne of ore translates to a nitrogen capture of just over 99.8 percent of the NOx from the thermal decomposition of magnesium nitrate. The process models developed in this exercise assume total conversion of the NOx from the thermal decomposition of magnesium nitrate, to nitric acid. This would seem to be an aspect of the nitrate circuit that merits the appropriate attention (if it has not already…). 

A similar argument can be made about the chloride circuit, of course. A difference between the chloride circuit and the nitrate circuit, though, is that in the chloride circuit hydrochloric acid is not decomposed and reconstituted as is the case in the nitrate circuit. In the chloride circuit the recovery of acid depends on efficient scrubbing of the various vapour streams, which is affected by the amounts of steam condensed with the acid in the scrubbers. More water condensed means better acid capture, but that water has to be re-evaporated, leading to a trade-off between acid loss and energy cost. In this exercise, the acid capture has been assumed to be efficient, as has the reconstitution of nitric acid from the nitrogen oxides. These assumptions would need to be verified, should these circuits ever be considered for any real project. 

In reality, other aspects of the three processes would also need to be considered, especially the capital expenditure. Three recent HPAL plants, (Ravensthorpe, Goro and Ambat

ovy) all came in with expenditures of >$3 billion for plants producing in the order of 50 000 tonnes of nickel. On its website, Direct Nickel quotes $500-600 million for a plant producing 20 000 tonnes of nickel, which extrapolates to $0.8-1.0 billion for a 50 000 tonne plant<sup>(12)</sup> . Order of magnitude capital cost estimates for a Neomet plant are of the same magnitude as the Direct Nickel estimate. The 

33 

atmospheric processes appear, at this level of estimate, to have a clear capital advantage over the HPAL option. 

Whilst chloride plants have, and continue to be, operated commercially, there are no commercial large-scale operations using nitric acid.  Noranda operated the Brenda Leach Process, employing a high temperature (105-110<sup>°</sup> C), high-strength chloride (CaCl₂, NaCl, HCl) atmospheric leach of copper-molybdenum sulphide concentrates until the mine shut down in the 1990s<sup>(13)</sup> . Xstrata (Falconbridge) operates a chloride process at its nickel-cobalt refinery in Kristiansand, Norway, which was initially a hydrochloric acid leach, but more recently a chlorine leach<sup>(14,15,16)</sup> . These and other plants such as those operated by Jinchuan<sup>(17)</sup> , Sumitomo<sup>(18)</sup> and SLN<sup>(19)</sup> in a mixed chloridesulphate medium, demonstrate that chloride-based circuits are perfectly feasible, and that any material-handling issues associated with a chloride environment can be and are being overcome. 

Nitrate plants are generally small-scale, such as for silver refining or the production of molybdic oxide. A problem in operating nitrate processes is the tendency for “runaway” reactions, particularly during leaching if there are minerals present that catalyze the decomposition of nitric acid. Balancing that, the issue of materials of construction may well be simpler for a nitrate circuit than for a chloride circuit. 

There are also the minor elements, notably calcium, sodium, potassium and manganese, which have not been considered in this exercise. In sulphate circuits, these are easily handled, generally reporting to a magnesium sulphate effluent, although manganese can co-precipitate with the MHP. In chloride circuits, all of these elements report through to the magnesium hydrolysis stage. Calcium is easily controlled via sulphate addition, and both potassium and sodium can be selectively crystallized from the magnesium hydrolysis filtrate, whereas manganese is conveniently oxidized to MnO2. 

In nitrate circuits, these impurities will behave similarly to their behavior in the chloride circuit, except that manganese will partially deport to the MHP product. Calcium nitrate would deport to the MgO product, representing a loss of nitrate and degrading the MgO purity, if calcium cannot be controlled by sulphate addition. Potassium and sodium could be problematic, as they decompose at a lower temperature than magnesium nitrate to the nitrite (a factor made use of in gunpowder), and could also repre

sent a loss of nitrogen to the MgO product. 

Finally, there is the issue of ferric nitrate, present in the leach solution in large quantities. Previous testwork has been reported showing that copper could be hydrolysed from silver nitrate solutions at 180°C<sup>(20)</sup> . Although not reported at that time, ferric nitrate was found to be unpredictable in its behaviour, which is consistent with its description in its MSDS that it can explode when heated<sup>21)</sup> . This is not to say that it will do so, just that there is the potential as with many nitrate solutions, and therefore that there might be risks associated with the use of nitrates which are not present with chloride or sulphate. 

###### **CONCLUSION** 

From the numbers emanating from the process models developed for this study, it would seem that both the chloride and the nitrate circuits examined have appreciably lower variable operating costs than the sulphate circuit. The reason is that the chloride and the nitrate circuits regenerate and recycle the acid used in the leach, while the sulphate circuit does not. The largest component of the variable cost in the nitrate and chloride circuits is energy. In this exercise natural gas was assumed as a heating utility, at a cost of $4/GJ. Since this is the dominant variable cost, the economics of any real project using either chloride or nitrate chemistry would be sensitive to the cost of energy. 

The numbers generated in this exercise give the chloride process a somewhat lower variable cost than the nitrate process, because the chloride process has a lower evaporation load and therefore a lower energy demand. However, if the nitrate circuit can be modified to use less water, its energy cost would be reduced significantly. 

HPAL technology has reached commercial operation, and therefore the problems associated with its operation are well known and understood. This is not so for the chloride and nitrate processes, which are in the development stage. There may be more comfort with chloride, since there are large-scale commercial operations using most aspects of the process. The key component of the chloride process, hydrolysis, has been extensively tested by Neomet. It has also been scaled up by a factor of five, twice. Similarly, the key aspects of the nitrate process are being piloted in Perth. 

Downward pressure on the cost of nickel production is unlikely to diminish. New nickel extraction technology that offers lower costs must be of value to the industry and to society. Both the chloride 

34 

and the nitrate processes examined in this exercise appear to appreciably reduce the cost of nickel production, at least relative to HPAL technology. One or both of these processes may well unlock laterite nickel that would otherwise remain in the ground.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The utilisation of MgO as a precipitant for base metals has increased significantly over the past 5 years, due to the relatively high grade base metal product that can be achieved when compared to lime. However, most base metal operations have found that the Mg content in the final product could be as high as 10-20% m/m Mg. This has major cost implications for an on-site refinery or for the sale and transport of an intermediate base metal hydroxide product. Reasons for the elevated Mg grades were identified as mode of reagent addition, precipitation temperature, ageing effects of MgO, as well as the grind size of the MgO. A suitable process route has been designed that improves the grade of the final mixed base metal hydroxide product by minimising the Mg content of the final product. A robust method for the determination of MgO reactivity within a typical base metal precipitation circuit is also discussed. 

37 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The use of MgO as a precipitant for base metal precipitation is attractive as it does not dilute the product with gypsum as is the case when using lime. Certain aspects around the use of MgO as precipitant for base metals have to be considered to optimise its economic performance. These aspects are mainly linked to an efficient reagent usage and a relatively low contamination of the final product with Mg. 

MgO used in hydrometallurgical applications would ideally be of a fine grind size (P100 of <45µm). At such fine grinds, the MgO particles have the tendency to agglomerate (caking). Exposure to ambient humidity may be a main contributing factor. If the reagent is added as bulk dry material to the base metal feed solution, the base metal could precipitate on the surface of the agglomerated particles, thereby coating the particle and prevent further reactivity. This could also occur during precipitation with lime. 

In order to overcome this it must either be ensured that no agglomerates of MgO form during addition of dry reagent, or the MgO should be added as a homogenous slurry, which would be the more effective approach. Test work was done in order to identify the optimum conditions for the addition of MgO as a slurry. It is suspected that MgO forms brucite once slurried with water, which then renders the MgO unreactive. 

###### **EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES** 

All experiments were conducted in 5L polypropylene reactors with mechanical agitation. Agitation was facilitated by overhead stirrers fitted with a flat blade turbine (4FBT, 0.6x reactor diameter, 400rpm). The reactors

were fitted with thermocouples for temperature control and heating was facilitated with steam coils. The lid was also equipped with ports for the measuring equipment and reagent addition. In the case of MgO powder addition, the reactor covers were removed for the period of MgO addition and thereafter refitted. 

###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** 

Precipitation of cobalt or other base metals with MgO occurs according to Equation1. 

_Equation 1_ 

_5CoSO4 + 4MgO + 4H2O→Co5(OH)8SO4 + 4MgSO4_ 

It may be noted here that the metal generally does not precipitate as pure hydroxide, but much rather as a hydroxy-sulphate. The metal hydroxy-sulphate to metal hydroxide ratio may vary according to operating conditions. Through the range of test conditions applied for the work described in this text the ratio was typically 60:40 in favour of the cobalt hydroxide. 

###### **Optimisation of Operating Conditions** 

MgO from two commercially available suppliers were tested for the purpose of this investigation, and will hereon be referred to as MgO 1 (95.3% m/m Mg), P80-19µm) and MgO 2 (88.5% m/m MgO, P80-30µm). MgO 2 was used to conduct all the optimisation testwork.

Synthetic liquor consisting of approximately 10g/L Co<sup>+2</sup> was prepared as the feed material. Initially three precipitation tests were conducted at 30<sup>o</sup> C, 50<sup>o</sup> C, and 70<sup>o</sup> C. According to Monhemius and previous test work conducted at Mintek, cobalt is precipitated as a hydroxide at a pH of approximately 8-8.5 (at 25<sup>o</sup> C). For purpose of this investigation, MgO was slurried in water to 20% m/m solids immediately before commencing each test. The pH of the solution was increased incrementally to 8.5 with the addition of 20% m/m MgO slurry in 0.5 hour increments over a period of 3.75 hours from a stirred reactor. Figure 1 illustrates the extent of precipitation and the purity of the precipitates formed with regard to Co/Mg for the different operating temperatures investigated.

Regarding the second test, MgO was added as a powder at a fixed rate for a period of 6 hours to the Co solution over a period of 6 hours. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

To date the only nickel laterite acid leaching plants constructed have been based around high pressure acid leaching (HPAL) technology and the only other nickel laterite hydrometallurgical plants constructed have employed the Caron process. Several downstream recovery routes have been employed, including mixed sulphide precipitation (MSP), mixed hydroxide precipitation (MHP) and direct solvent extraction (DSX), with commercial products ranging from intermediates (MSP/MHP) to nickel oxide, nickel briquettes and nickel cathodes. Over the last decade considerable effort has been expended on the development of atmospheric and low pressure leaching   processes (heap leaching and agitated tank leaching), as well as integrated flowsheets that re-generate the lixiviant and produce value-adding by-products. Much progress has been made towards the development of alternative downstream recovery processes, particularly in the field of DSX. 

This paper examines trends and new developments in hydrometallurgical processing of nickel laterite ores. Block flowsheets for the established and developmental processes are presented and the relative merits of each flowsheet are discussed. 

45 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The last two decades have seen unprecedented interest in the development of new hydrometallurgical processes for nickel laterites, due to the depletion of nickel sulphide ore reserves and the limitations of ferro-nickel smelting, particularly in terms of treating limonitic ores. These new developments have centred chiefly around acid leaching technologies and the downstream processes to recover nickel and cobalt from acid leach liquors. 

This paper aims to introduce the reader to a broad cross-section

of the hydrometallurgical processing options available for nickel laterites and to provide some broad guidelines to aid preliminary selection of the most appropriate process flowsheet for a particular project. A wide cross-section of leaching technologies and downstream processing options are reviewed. 

###### **LEACHING TECHNOLOGIES** 

The two principal hydrometallurgical treatment processes for nickel laterite ores to have been commercialised are the Caron process and the High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) process. Both of these processing routes were first employed in plants that were commissioned in Cuba by the Freeport Sulfur Company. 

This paper will primarily discuss acid leaching technologies, which include the better known sulphuric acid leach processes: 

- HPAL 

- HPAL + Saprolite Neutralisation 

- Atmospheric Leaching 

- HPAL + Atmospheric Leaching + Saprolite Neutralisation 

- EPAL 

- Heap Leaching 

as well as more recent developments that substantially regenerate and recycle the lixiviant and produce magnesia from the magnesium that is extracted from the ore: 

- Direct Nickel 

- CFNP (Carbon Friendly Nickel Process) 

- Nichromet 

- Neomet 

###### **The Caron Process** 

The Caron process, as employed at Nicaro (Cuba), Niquelandia (Brazil), Nonoc (Philippines, closed), Punta-Gorda (Cuba) and QNI (Australia), uses atmospheric ammonia leaching of reduced nickel ore and predates the HPAL process. The first plant was operated for the US Government by Nicaro Nickel Co. between 1944 and 1947. The feed iron content required by the Caron process limits its use to limonitic ores or a mixture of limonite and saprolite. The ore is dried and nickel is selectively reduced (together with cobalt and some iron) to metallic nickel via a reduction roast at approximately 750°C. The metals are subsequently extracted by leaching in an 

ammonia/ammonium carbonate solution. Recovery decreases with increasing saprolite content as nickel and cobalt are incorporated within a silicate matrix and rendered more difficult to reduce. The process is, however, more tolerant of magnesium than HPAL. The Caron process suffers from two key disadvantages: (i) the front-end of the process is pyrometallurgical, involving energy intensive drying, calcining and reduction steps and (ii) nickel and cobalt recoveries are generally lower than for smelting or HPAL.  (Dalvi, Bacon & Osborne, 2004). 

As the front-end is essentially pyrometallurgical, the Caron process will not be discussed in any further detail in this paper. 

46 

###### **High Pressure Acid Leaching (HPAL)** 

###### **_Overview_** 

HPAL has been employed to treat nickel laterite ores since the start-up of the Moa Nickel plant in Cuba in 1959. To this day it remains the only acid leaching technology for nickel laterites to have actually been commercialised as a start-up project. HPAL has been employed at Moa Bay (Cuba), Murrin Murrin (WA), Cawse (WA, closed), Bulong (WA, closed), Coral Bay (Philipp

ines), Vale Nouvelle-Calйdonie (New Caledonia), Ravensthorpe (WA), Ramu (PNG) and Ambatovy (Madagascar), and will also be employed at Taganito (Philippines) which is under construction. 

HPAL typically involves leaching of the laterite ore in concentrated sulphuric acid at temperatures in excess of 240°C. At these temperatures sulphuric acid reacts with ore constituents in many complex reactions. Substantial amounts of all metals are leached from the ore, however due to the low solubility of hematite, Fe2O3, and hydronium alunite, (H3O)Al3(SO4)2(OH)6, at elevated temperature, the majority of the iron (III) and aluminium are re-precipitated. These precipitation reactions also regenerate acid. This conveys two key advantages to HPAL over lower temperature leaching     processes for nickel laterite: (i) significantly lower acid consumption due to minimal net acid        requirement for iron and aluminium chemistry, and (ii) vastly better solid-liquid separation properties of a hematite dominated leach residue. 

Due to the advantageous high temperature reaction chemistry, HPAL is best suited to limonitic ores that are by definition high in iron. High magnesium ores can be problematic since magnesium is substantially leached, forming magnesium sulphate which exhibits inverse solubility at elevated temperatures, leading to heavy scaling. As saprolitic ores are usually high in magnesium, this usually means that saprolite must be diluted with limonite to provide a satisfactory magnesium grade in HPAL feed. The magnesium limit varies with other mineralogy and leach chemistry factors, but is generally in the 4.5-5.5% range. HPAL typically extracts at least 95% of the contained nickel and cobalt, with acid consumptions in the range 250-400 kg per tonne of ore for limonites and up to 550 kg per tonne of ore for limonite/saprolite blends. 

###### **_Applicability of the Flowsheet_** 

As there is a limit to the amount of magnesium that can be tolerated by the leaching process, HPAL as a standalone leaching technology is best suited to limonite dominated orebodies that permit saprolite to be blended into leach feed without exceeding 4.5-5.5% magnesium in the feed blend. Deposits where saprolite has been selectively mined for ferro-nickel production are ideally suited (e.g. Coral Bay). 

###### **_Brief Process Description_** 

For the purposes of this discussion the HPAL specific process steps are ore preparation, slurry heating, leaching, slurry pressure letdown and counter-current decantation (CCD). The major process steps involved are summarised below: 

###### _Ore Preparation_ 

Generally a feed size of 250-500 microns is preferred for HPAL. A ball mill is usually required to achieve the desired feed size as limonite ore in particular does not contain sufficient coarse to support SAG milling. Since nickel is normally associated with goethite (iron) minerals, and these tend to be fines, it is frequently possible to upgrade nickel content and reject sili

ca, and in some cases magnesium, by de-agglomeration (e.g. scrubbing) and classification (e.g. screening or cyclones). Fines are directed to leach feed thickening while oversize fractions are either milled or rejected as appropriate. 

Since HPAL throughput is residence time based, hydraulic flowrate is an important factor in determining the autoclave size. It is therefore important to achieve the highest possible solids content in leach feed slurry, so maximization of feed slurry % solids is a key design priority to minimise autoclave cost. 

47 

###### _Slurry Heating_ 

The HPAL feed slurry is heated through a three stage direct contact heating process prior to pressure acid leaching (can be typically two or four stages). In each stage the slurry is heated by condensing flash steam vented from the corresponding flash vessel. In the final stage high temperature (HT) splash vessel, the slurry is heated by condensing sufficient steam vented from the HP flash vessel to maintain the design slurry exit temperature (190-205°C). The maximum slurry temperature is governed by the temperature limitations of the positive displacement piston diaphragm autoclave feed pumps. 

###### _Leaching_ 

HPAL autoclaves are horizontal, titanium clad carbon steel vessels that are usually divided into six compartments, each of which is equipped with a titanium agitator. Slurry overflows from one compartment to the next, based on stepped compartment wall heights. The agitators employ pitched blade axial flow impellers to provide solids suspension, and to aid acid and steam mixing and reaction with the slurry. The agitator seals require dedicated seal barrier water and flush water systems for operation. 

In the autoclave, concentrated sulphuric acid (98.5 % w/w) and high pressure saturated steam (typically 265-275°C) are injected to achieve the desired leaching conditions under which almost all of the nickel and cobalt solids are leached from the ore. The simplified key leaching reactions are: 

|Al(OH)3|→|AlOOH + H2O (in preheaters)|
|---|---|---|
|2 AlOOH + 3 H2SO4|→|Al2(SO4)3+ 4 H2O|
|2 FeO(OH) + 3 H2SO4|→|Fe2(SO4)3+ 4 H2O|
|NiO + H2SO4|→|NiSO4+ H2O|
|CoO + H2SO4|→|CoSO4+ H2O|
|MgO + H2SO4|→|MgSO4+ H2O|
|MnO + H2SO4|→|MnSO4+ H2O|
|ZnO + H2SO4|→|ZnSO4+ H2O|
|CuO + H2SO4|→|CuSO4+ H2O|
|SiO2.H2O|→|SiO2+ H2O|
|SiO2+ 2 H2O|→|H4SiO4|
|Cr2O3+ 3 H2SO4|→|Cr2(SO4)3+ 3 H2O|



Re-precipitation of iron occurs via hydrolysis to hematite and possibly hydronium jarosite: 

|Fe2(SO4)3+ 3 H2O|→|Fe2O3+ 3 H2SO4|
|---|---|---|
|3 Fe2(SO4)3+ 14 H2O|→|2 (H3O)Fe3(SO4)2(OH)6+ 5 H2SO4|



Re-precipitation of aluminium occurs via hydrolysis to alunite: 

3 Al2(SO4)3 + 14 H2O → 2 (H3O)Al3(SO4)2(OH)6 + 5 H2SO4 

The apparent formation of hydronium jarosite is most likely a result of substitution of iron into alunite, typically at about 20-30% replacement of aluminium. 

In the presence of sodium chloride (e.g. if either saline ground water or sea water is used in ore preparation) precipitatio

n of natro-jarosite and sodium alunite may also take place: 

3 Fe2(SO4)3 + 2 NaCl + 12 H2O → 2 NaFe3(SO4)2(OH)6 + 5 H2SO4 + 2 HCl 3 Al2(SO4)3 + 2 NaCl + 12 H2O → 2 NaAl3(SO4)2(OH)6 + 2 HCl + 5 H2SO4 

The quantity of magnesium in the ore and the extent of re-precipitation of iron and aluminium largely govern the consumption of sulphuric acid. 

Acid is pumped into the autoclaves by the sulphuric acid dosing pumps and tantalum dip-tubes are used for acid injection. In the event of valve failure the main sulphuric acid storage is protected from slurry contamination by both the positive displacement pumps and a day tank. The steam system is protected from slurry blow back by a steam blow back vessel. 

48 

Non-condensable gases generated in the autoclave are bled from the autoclave vapour space to the vent gas scrubber to maintain the autoclave overpressure within design limits. An overpressure of approximately 500 kPa is recommended to prevent the slurry from flashing in the autoclave discharge line prior to entering the autoclave discharge level control valve, physically located on the HP flash vessel. The autoclave operating conditions are typically 240-260°C and 4400-5000 kPa pressure. 

A sketch of the leaching circuit is shown in Figure 1. 



**Figure 1: HPAL Process Flowsheet** 

###### _Slurry Pressure Letdown_ 

The leached slurry is progressively depressurized through a three stage pressure letdown process (can be two or four stages). The hot slurry discharges from the autoclave through a ceramic lined choke valve on the HP flash vessel that maintains a constant slurry level in the last compartment. The slurry is progressively depressurized through the HP, MP and LP flash vessels to atmospheric pressure by flashing off steam, which is recycled to the HPAL feed slurry heaters. The last flash vessel discharges into the flash seal tank which ensures the slurry is at atmospheric pressure. 

All excess flash steam, non-condensable purges, emergency shutdown vents and the safety relief system are directed to the HPAL vent scrubber system where any acid entrainment is removed through a combination of centrifugal separation and venturi scrubbing. The cleaned steam is released to atmosphere. 

###### _CCD Circuit_ 

Slurry from the leach circuit is fed to a CCD circuit where leached residue is washed countercurrently to recover soluble nickel and cobalt values. Typically 6 or 7 CCD stages are required. The wash solution is usually pH adjusted barren process solution from the downstream recovery areas. Better settling characteristics are usually achieved if the slurry pH is kept sufficiently low to substantially avoid the precipitation of any metal hydroxides. 

49 

The main function of the CCD circuit is to recover soluble nickel and cobalt from the leach residue solids. This is achieved by counter current washing of the leached solids with barren wash solution to recover dissolved nickel and cobalt values. The nickel and cobalt rich liquor fro

m the first CCD thickener overflow is forwarded to the downstream purification and recovery circuits. The underflow from the last thickener is typically discharged to the final neutralization area. 

###### **HPAL plus Saprolite Neutralisation** 

###### **_Overview_** 

As discussed previously, HPAL is best suited to limonitic ores that are by definition high in iron. High magnesium ores can be problematic since magnesium is substantially leached forming magnesium sulphate which exhibits inverse solubility at elevated temperatures, leading to heavy scaling. As saprolitic ores are usually high in magnesium, this means that saprolite must be diluted with limonite to provide a satisfactory magnesium grade for HPAL feed. The magnesium limit varies with other leach factors, but is typically in the range of 4.5-5.5%. A practical option is to use reactive high magnesium saprolite ore to partially neutralize the excess acid in HPAL discharge. 

Historically the flashed HPAL discharge slurry has been neutralised using limestone however a recent trend in flowsheet design is to replace limestone with high acid consuming (e.g. high magnesium) saprolite ore, a process commonly referred to as Saprolite Neutralisation. This minimises process limestone consumption and provides the added benefit of simultaneously extracting additional nickel values (typically 60-90% nickel extraction) from saprolitic material that may have otherwise been unsuitable for processing. 

The concept of saprolite neutralization is a common sense one that has been widely considered for nickel laterite projects dating back at least as far as the Amax Process patented in the late 1970’s and the SURAL process developed by Sulzer in the 1980’s which was evaluated for the Gasquet Mountain Project (California Nickel Corporation). Since the re-birth of HPAL in the mid-1990’s saprolite neutralisation has been investigated for a number of proposed HPAL projects. “Saprolite acid-kill” was tested at Hazen Research for the Nonoc HPAL Conversion study in 1998, and saprolite neutralisation has been tested for several other projects since, including Weda Bay (Indonesia), Sulawesi (Indonesia), Gladstone (Australia), Mindoro (Philippines), Berong (Philippines) and Agata (Philippines). 

###### **_Applicability of the Flowsheet_** 

Typically the ratio of saprolite neutralisation feed to HPAL feed must be less than 0.4 : 1. Beyond this proportion three key issues arise: (i) the quantity of saprolite ore exceeds the available free acid, (ii) a sharp decrease in nickel extraction from the saprolite is observed, and (iii) a sharp deterioration in CCD settling performance occurs. The HPAL-Saprolite Neutralisation flowsheet is therefore best suited to limonite dominated orebodies in which the proportion of limonite to saprolite exceeds 2 to 1. 

###### **_Brief Process Description_** 

The process steps are limonite ore preparation, HPAL (heating, leach and letdown), saprolite ore preparation, saprolite neut

ralisation and CCD. The key process steps involved are outlined below: Limonite ore preparation and the HPAL circuit are described in the previous section. Preparation of saprolite ore for neutralisation can be relatively simple. Generally a feed size of 0.5-1.0 mm is satisfactory. A SAG mill can usually achieve the desired feed size as saprolite ore typically contains sufficient coarse material. Upgrading via de-agglomeration (e.g. scrubbing) and classification (e.g. screening or cyclones) is sometimes possible, however nickel tends to be more evenly deported across the size fractions in saprolite ore. HPAL discharge slurry is fed to the Saprolite Neutralisation circuit, where it is blended with highly acid-consuming high magnesium saprolite ore slurry to neutralise some of the residual free sulphuric acid. In addition to consuming much of the free acid, approximately 60-90% of the nickel and cobalt in the saprolite ore is extracted. Reactivity is best at 90-100°C. The acid concentration in the slurry exiting the saprolite neutralisation circuit is typically 10–15 g/L. 50 If either saline ground water or sea water is used in ore preparation the presence of sodium will result in some precipitation of natro-jarosite and sodium alunite as the free acid concentration decreases: 3 Fe2(SO4)3 + 2 NaCl + 12 H2O → 3 Al2(SO4)3 + 2 NaCl + 12 H2O → 2 NaFe3(SO4)2(OH)6 + 5 H2SO4 + 2 HCl 2 NaAl3(SO4)2(OH)6 + 2 HCl + 5 H2SO4 This opportune chemical behaviour reduces downstream limestone consumption and minimises the quantity of poorly settling iron and aluminium hydroxides from neutralisation to be dealt with in the back half of the CCD circuit. Saprolite neutralisation would most likely be performed in acid-brick lined carbon steel tanks. The discharge from the last saprolite neutralisation tank is forwarded to the CCD circuit. The nickel and cobalt rich liquor from the first CCD thickener overflow is forwarded to the downstream purification and recovery circuits. The underflow from the last thickener is typically discharged to the final neutralization area. An indicative HPAL-Saprolite Neutralisation flowsheet is shown in Figure 2. MAKE-UP WATER

Limonite ores are therefore extremely unsuitable for AL as they consume phenomenal quantit

ies of acid due to their high iron content and the absence of re-precipitation reactions that regenerate acid. In addition, very high ferric sulphate tenors in leach solution cause viscosity and solubility issues downstream. AL is therefore best suited to saprolitic ores that are by definition low in iron. The concerns about magnesium content associated with saprolite in HPAL do not apply to AL as the inverse solubility problem associated with magnesium sulphate at elevated temperature does not impact on AL, which operates at below 105°C. 

AL typically extracts at least 90% of the contained nickel and cobalt. The amount of iron and aluminium present is still sufficient to account for considerably higher acid consumption than HPAL, however acid consumption for saprolite AL is typically 800-1000 kg per tonne of ore depending on the iron, magnesium and aluminium grades. For high grade saprolites this can translate to a similar acid consumption per tonne of contained nickel to that of limonite HPAL, rendering AL an economic and low capital cost option for such ores. 

During the late 1990’s BHP Billiton conducted considerable R&D into AL resulting in a patented process based on a two-stage atmospheric leach flowsheet. In the first stage a limonite ore slurry at between 5% and 35% solids is leached using sulphuric acid, with the addition of sulphur dioxide gas as a reductant to maintain a redox potential of 900-1000 mV (SHE). Saprolite ore slurry is introduced to the second stage and combined with the discharge from the first stage, along with the addition of alkali metal or ammonium ions to promote precipitation of iron as jarosite. Some of the precipitates are separated and recycled as seed to the second stage. 

Gladstone Pacific Nickel patented a two-stage counter-current atmospheric leach process, in which the second stage discharge is thickened and the thickener overflow used as an acid recycle to the first stage. This process is designed, however, to be coupled with a HPAL circuit, as one of the feed streams to the second stage thickener is HPAL discharge slurry. 

AL process flowsheets are currently proposed for the Weda Bay (Indonesia), Dutwa (Tanzania) and Zambales (Philippines) projects. 

###### **_Applicability of the Flowsheet_** 

AL in its basic form is not suited to limonite ores as their high iron content results in high acid consumption and excessive ferric sulphate concentrations in leach solution. Some more sophisticated AL technologies employ proprietary iron precipitation techniques to partially alleviate these problems. With the exception of these proprietary processes, AL is best suited to ores with low iron content, generally saprolites. It is therefore best suited to saprolite dominated orebodies that contain very little limonite, or orebodies in which limonite grades are so low that commercial treatment is not justifiable.

Some upgrading via de-agglomeration (e.g. scrubbing) and classification (e.g. screening or cyclones) may be possible, however it is generally not warranted for an AL process as the costs of additional leach tanks to treat a larger quantity of feed are incremental and more than offset by the amount of nickel lost with beneficiation reject material. The agitators employ pitched blade axial flow impellers to provide solids suspension, and to aid acid and steam mixing and reaction with the slurry. Slurry overflows from one tank to the next. ###### **HPAL and Atmospheric Leach (AL) plus Saprolite Neutralisation** 

###### **_Overview_** 

_NOTE: This flowsheet is sometimes mistakenly referred to as EPAL. It is not. It is in fact a simple and common-sense precursor to EPAL, which has additional features and is discussed separately later._ 

As discussed previously, HPAL is best suited to limonitic ores, with the possibility of blending a small amount of saprolite into the leach feed. Integrating a saprolite neutralisation circuit enables the processing of orebodies with a limonite to saprolite ratio in excess of 2 to 1. However it is not uncommon for a nickel laterite orebodies to have a roughly 1 to 1 limonite to saprolite ratio, or even to be saprolite dominated. In these scenarios the inclusion of a parallel atmospheric leach (AL) circuit for high grade saprolite is recommended. AL is best suited to saprolitic ores with low iron and preferably high nickel grade (refer to AL above). 

The optimal flowsheet for a 1:1 or saprolite dominated orebody thus combines HPAL for limonite and parallel AL for high grade saprolite, with the leach discharge streams combined for saprolite neutralisation using low grade, high magnesium saprolite ore. The cut off between high and low grade saprolite will be project specific and should be established by testwork aimed at maximising nickel recovery and optimising neutralisation of free acid and CCD settling performance. 

The concept of HPAL-AL-Saprolite Neutralisation is a common sense one that has been considered in various forms for a number of nickel laterite projects dating back at least as far as the Amax Process patented in the late 1970’s. The flowsheet as described has been tested for several projects including Weda Bay (Indonesia), Sulawesi (Indonesia), Gladstone (Australia), Mindoro (Philippines) and Agata (Philippines). 

###### **_Applicability of the Flowsheet_** 

As with the HPAL plus saprolite neutralisation flowsheet, typically the ratio of saprolite neutralisation feed to combined HPAL and AL feed must be less than 0.4 : 1. Beyond this proportion three key issues arise: (i) the quantity of saprolite neutralisation feed exceeds the available free acid in the combined leach discharge, (ii) a sharp decrease in nickel extraction from the saprolite neutralisation feed is observed, and (iii) a sharp deterioration in CCD settling performance occurs. There are however no strict limitations on the relative proportions of HPAL and AL feed, so generally the saprolite ore can be distributed between AL and saprolite neutralisation in a manner which enables

the desired HPAL + AL : Saprolite Neutralisation feed ratio to be achieved. ###### **_Brief Process Description_** The HPAL, AL and Saprolite Neutralisation circuits are described in the previous sections. ###### **Heap Leaching** 

###### **_Overview_** 

Nickel laterite heap leaching has been investigated since at least the late 1970’s. The first major R&D program was undertaken at NTUA (National Technical University of Athens) in Greece during the 1990’s, involving column leaches of Greek laterite ores. A small demonstration plant was constructed at the Larco mine site. 

Interest soared during the last decade on the back of development work undertaken by European Nickel at Зaldağ, in Western Turkey, which included a successful demonstration plant. Considerable research was also conducted by Metallica Minerals, BHP-Billiton, Vale Inco and Minara Resources among others. Minara subsequently developed the only nickel laterite heap leach to have been operated at a commercial scale, with downstream processing and key services and infrastructure provided by the adjacent Murrin Murrin HPAL project. To date no standalone nickel laterite heap leach projects have been brought into operation on a commercial scale. Some projects initially put forward as heap leach projects have ultimately selected alternative leaching technologies, e.g. ENK’s Zambales (previously Acoje) Project in the Philippines and African Eagle’s Dutwa Nickel Project in Tanzania have both been recast as atmospheric leach projects. 

A major obstacle to successfully heap leaching laterites is that typically between 20 and 30% of the ore is dissolved to achieve a nickel recovery in the range 65 to 75%, as compared with 1 to 3% in a typical copper heap leaching project. Two impacts of this are comparatively high acid consumption and the related destruction of the permeability-enhancing agglomerates. Permeability decreases, often by a factor of up to 100, and this can be further aggravated by re-precipitation of iron compounds.  (Steemson, 2009) The Зaldağ laterites have a low clay content which contributes to better permeability. In the Greek and Зaldağ laterites iron is present mostly as hematite rather than goethite. This is advantageous for preserving the structure of the heap as unlike goethite there is little dissolution and mass loss from hematite. 

The case for heap leaching is based on lower capital costs in comparison to HPAL, however this argument is fundamentally flawed. A heap leach plant substitutes HPAL and CCD with the Heap Leach circuit but all of the remaining process, services, utilities and infrastructure are still required. The real capital cost saving for a heap leach project over an equivalent HPAL project is between 15 and 20%. Heap leach metal recoveries are 15-20% lower than HPAL recoveries, so a 15-20% loss of revenue must be sacrificed **every year** for an upfront saving of less than 20%. 

Various parties have been awarded patents for nickel laterite heap leaching processes including Greek researc

hers, ENK (formerly European Nickel), BHP Billiton, Vale and Metallica Minerals. 

###### **_Applicability of the Flowsheet_** 

Due to its substantially lower metal recoveries than HPAL or AL, heap leaching is best suited to low grade laterites or small orebodies that do not justify a HPAL or AL project of an economic size. Heap leaching is generally not well suited to limonite ores as they contain a high proportion of fines and their high iron content results in high mass loss and breakdown of the heap structure / agglomerates. Hematite rich limonites are an exception. Saprolites are generally more suitable as they have a lower proportion of fines and a high silica content which usually translates to lower mass loss. Some ores such as Metallica Minerals’ Minnamoolka and Bell Creek laterites in North Queensland have a “silica boxwork” structure that helps to maintain structure and permeability of the heap (see Figure 5). 

56 

Coarse material such as oversize reject from a laterite ore beneficiation plant is also well suited to heap leaching. 



**Figure 5: Silica Boxwork Ore Type (source: Metallica Minerals Website)** 

###### **_Brief Process Description_** 

The process steps in a heap leach flowsheet are ore preparation, agglomeration and heap leaching. No CCD circuit is required. The key process steps involved are outlined below. 

The ore is crushed to a suitable size and forwarded to an agglomeration drum, or agglomerator. The function of the agglomerator is to wet and mix the ore with concentrated sulphuric acid and in some cases a binder. The agglomerates, when cured, are stable during heap leaching. The stability of the cured agglomerates is critical for enabling the heap leach to operate with high permeability. A second function of agglomeration is acid curing of the ores to promote rapid initial leaching kinetics when heap leaching commences. 

Following agglomeration, the agglomerated ore is transported to the heap. Discharged agglomerates are directed onto an overland conveyor which transports the agglomerates to the leach pad feed conveyor. The overland conveyor delivers the ore to a stacker which runs and stacks the ore from the one end to the other until the leach module is complete. On completing each module it returns to the start-end of the next module and re-commences stacking. 

After stacking, the agglomerate is subjected to rest and curing in the leach pad area, while the irrigation net is installed. After curing, moisturizing is carried out at a slow flowrate over a number of days in order to preserve heap stability. 

Each heap module is leached in a series of stages to utilise its acid neutralising capacity, extract the nickel into solution and to rinse and prepare the heap for decommissioning. Once a module is decommissioned the spent ore is removed and fresh ore stacked. Alternatively, if the spent ore is geotechnically stable, the next module may be stacked on top of the spent ore. 

A counter-current configuratio

n is usually selected for the process in order to enhance nickel concentration in the solution, with the final PLS contacting the freshest ore. The leach cycle is divided into two main parts: primary leaching and secondary leaching. At the end of the cycle, the depleted heap leach ore is rinsed with barren liquor in order to recover nickel and cobalt in solution. The cycle consists of heap leach, stacking, curing, moisturising, primary leach secondary leach, washing with barren liquor and final drainage. A typical flowsheet is shown in Figure 6. 

57 

PLS is collected via a drainage system installed beneath each leach module. As the PLS is essentially solids-free there is no requirement for a CCD circuit and instead it may be forwarded directly to downstream processing. 

Heap leach kinetics for nickel laterites are generally slow, with cycle times of up to 1.5 years or even more. This means that a large land area is required because a very long time has to elapse before any spent leach modules can be replaced. 



**Figure 6: Typical Counter-Current Heap Leach Flowsheet (source: Readett & Fox, ALTA 2009)** 

###### **Direct Nickel Process** 

###### **_Overview_** 

The Direct Nickel (DNi) Process is an atmospheric leach process that is capable of treating the full laterite profile (from limonitic to saprolitic ores). This ability to treat the full lateritic profile potentially offers the opportunity to commercialize deposits that are considered uneconomic. 

The DNi Process uses nitric acid to leach nickel laterite ores, extracting most metals into solution and leaving a silicate leach residue. A key feature of the DNi Process is the ability to recover more than 95% of the lixiviant for re-use in the process, significantly reducing operating costs, whilst extracting the majority of the nickel and cobalt from the ore. An advantage of nitric acid is the high solubility of its metal salts compared to sulphuric and hydrochloric acids, allowing higher solution tenors. This can reduce hydraulic flowrates resulting in potentially lower capital costs compared with equivalent metal extractions by the other two acids. There are additional advantages with some elements, such as calcium where the nitrate is soluble but the sulphate produces gypsum, often causing scaling and deposition. 

###### **_Applicability of the Flowsheet_** 

Direct Nickel claim that the process is suitable for treatment of all types of laterite ore combined into a single feed stream, offering a single process to treat the full laterite resource. As the requirements for make-up reagents are relatively low, the DNi process appears to be an excellent option for remote locations. 

###### **_Brief Process Description_** 

The major steps in the DNi process flowsheet are leaching, CCD, iron hydrolysis, intermediate product precipitation (IPP), IPP re-leach, aluminium hydrolysis, nickel/cobalt precipitation, barren decomposition and reagent recovery. The key features of the process are

outlined below. Leaching takes place in closed tanks at just above 100°C and with typically less than 5 hours residence time. More than 90% of the nickel, cobalt, manganese, magnesium and other base metals are extracted. Extraction of iron, aluminium and chromium depends largely on the 58 mineralogy of the ore feed. The leach discharge slurry is forwarded to a CCD circuit to separate the PLS from the leach residue. The PLS is concentrated by evaporation, after which a thermal hydrolysis process is employed to precipitate more than 99% of the iron and chromium in a hematite form. Subsequently recycled magnesia (MgO) is used to precipitate an intermediate product which contains the nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium and other base metals, leaving a barren solution containing mainly magnesium nitrate. The intermediate precipitate is separated from the barren solution by thickening and filtration and is subsequently re-leached. The re-leach PLS is heated to remove aluminium by thermal hydrolysis, and the pH of the aluminium-free solution is then raised using MgO to produce a high quality nickel/cobalt hydroxide product. If required the nickel and cobalt hydroxide can be further treated to produce an oxide or sulphide product. The barren solution containing in the order of 66-69% magnesium nitrate hexahydrate is concentrated by evaporation at 200-215°C to form a magnesium nitrate melt with 1-2 moles of water. The melt is forwarded to a thermal decomposition unit and decomposed at 300°C, liberating NOx gases and producing MgO powder. The NOx gases are treated via a series of absorbers and scrubbers, recovering 99% of the NOx as a 55% nitric acid solution. The nitric acid and MgO are recycled within the process.
