The Ni content of a laterite ore body is typically 10 to 100 times greater than Co. The higher affinity of CYANEX 272 for Co over Ni permits the extraction of the lower concentration metal, which lowers the operating and capital costs of the SX plant (less NaOH or NH4

OH required for neutralization and a smaller initial organic fill). Eqn. 1 shows the extraction equilibrium for Co<sup>2+</sup> , in which two hydrogen-bonded phosphinic acid dimers each lose one proton to form the extracted complex. In the Ni laterite industry, however, the concentrations of Mn and Mg are higher than encountered in other Ni/Co separation applications. It is therefore important to review the processing options available to reject the impurity metals. Cytec has the capability to simulate Ni/Co separation CYANEX 272 SX circuits, enabling higher reagent utilization while maximizing metal separation<sup>(13)(14)</sup> . 



Mg, Ca and Mn rejection can be achieved by using H2S to form MSP, containing Ni, Co and Zn. The MSP can then be leached under pressure with O2 and H2SO4 to recover Ni and Co into solution, and residual Fe<sup>3+</sup> can be precipitated by NaOH addition. Zn can then be removed in an initial CYANEX 272 circuit, with a second CYANEX 272 circuit used to separate Co from Ni by extracting Co, using base for pH control. Using sulfuric acid to strip generates a Co-rich solution (pH 2.0-2.5) suitable for electrowinning or hydrogen reduction. The Ni-containing raffinate (pH 5.0-5.5) is at a suitable pH for metal recovery by hydrogen reduction<sup>(4)</sup> , while the pH must be adjusted to ~3.5 for Ni electrowinning<sup>15</sup> . The MSP-releach-CYANEX 272-H2 reduction route is used at Murrin Murrin<sup>(4)</sup> . This and other processing options are available to remove Mg and Mn from Co solutions, and are described in the context of African Cu-Co processing<sup>(16)</sup> . Mg removal prior to Co extraction is critical, since otherwise a large portion of the CYANEX 272 capacity would be taken up by Mg. 



**Figure 2: Extraction vs pH for CYANEX 272**<sup>**(17)**</sup> 

Unlike phosphinic acids, dithiophosphinic acids, such as CYANEX 301, can be used directly on a laterite PLS after Fe removal, due to the excellent rejection of Mn, Mg and Ca (Figure 3). The low pH of Ni and Co extraction eliminates the need for pH adjustment during extraction<sup>(18)</sup> . The strong co-extraction of Ni and Co does however necessitate a secondary Ni/Co separation step. At the Goro plant in New Caledonia, this is achieved by changing the medium from sulfate to chloride and separating Ni and Co using a tertiary amine reagent (see below). The change to chloride medium is accomplished by stripping Ni and Co from the loaded CYANEX 301 with 6 mol/L HCl at 60°C using a five minute mixing time<sup>(19)</sup> . These harsh stripping conditions are necessary due to the slow stripping kinetics of Ni.

In contrast to CYANEX 272, CYANEX 301 does not exist as dimers in the organic phase<sup>(7)</sup> , therefore, the extraction equilbria are different (Eqn.2 and Eqn. 3):

A significant challenge to the commercial use of CYANEX 301 is its reduced stability in the presence of oxidizing agents, including O2 and oxidizing metals such as Fe<sup>3+(18)</sup> . Oxidation proceeds from dithiophosphinic acid to monothiophosphinic through to phosphinic acid (Eqn. 4), which results in a loss of selectivity and strength. The Goro plant manages this issue by using very large pulsed columns to maintain an inert atmosphere<sup>(21)</sup> rather than open-air mixer-settlers to carry out the extraction and stripping. 





An additional consideration includes the susceptibility of Co to oxidation when extracted by dithiophosphinic acids, as evidenced by a change to the UV-visible spectrum and the difficulty of stripping Co after exposure to air<sup>(22)</sup> . Cu<sup>2+</sup> is also very difficult to strip if loaded, and consequently must be removed from the PLS down to very low levels by ion exchange prior to contact with the organic to avoid poisoning of the reagent<sup>(23)</sup> . 

###### **_Carboxylic Acids_** 

Carboxylic acids extract Ni by a proton exchange reaction, forming a complex containing undissociated acid molecules (Eqn. 5) which can then dimerize in the organic phase (Eqn. 6); Co behaves similarly to Ni<sup>(8)</sup> . 



196 

Carboxylic acids have good selectivity for Ni and Co over Mg, but suffer from poor selectivity against Ca. Co-extraction of Ca can cause gypsum precipitation in H2SO4 strip solutions. Significant aqueous solubility of the carboxylate at the extraction pH can lead to high losses of extractant unless a reagent recovery stage is included, which adds to the operating cost. 

###### **_Chelating Oxime Reagents_** 

In ammoniacal media, Ni and Co exist as mixtures of cationic ammine complexes (Eqn. 7)<sup>(24)</sup> . Depending on the concentration of ammonia, [Co(NH3)n]<sup>2+</sup> is not stable in ammoniacal solutions due to the presence of the strong-field ammine ligands, which results in a filled t2g subshell when lowspin d<sup>7</sup> Co<sup>2+</sup> is oxidized to low-spin d<sup>6</sup> Co<sup>3+</sup> , removing the orbital degeneracy of the low-spin d<sup>7</sup> state (Figure 5). This in fact forms the basis of Ni/Co separation in ammoniacal media, which relies on the kinetic differences between Ni<sup>2+</sup> and Co<sup>3+</sup> . Co<sup>3+</sup> is kinetically inert (see Figure 1) and is not extracted during the residence time in the mix-box (despite a high distribution ratio at equilibrium). In practice, e.g. at the Yabulu refinery in Townsville, Queensland<sup>(25)</sup> ,

[Co(NH3)n]<sup>2+</sup> is deliberately oxidized to [Co(NH3)n]<sup>3+</sup> with H2O2 to avoid extraction of Co. 

M<sup>2+</sup> + nNH3 = [M(NH3)n]<sup>2+</sup> ( 7 ) 









**Figure 5: Electronic Configurations of Co**<sup>**2+**</sup> **and Co**<sup>**3+**</sup> **in Ammonia (adapted from Cotton and Wilkinson**<sup>**(26)**</sup> **)** 

Ni extraction proceeds according to Eqn. 8, via deprotonation of the phenol and chelation of the phenolate oxygen and the oxime nitrogen. Since the extraction is in ammoniacal medium, ammonium ions are formed rather than protons, in a 2:1 L:M stoichiometry<sup>(10)</sup> . Ni stripping can be effected by reversing the equilibrium with strong NH3 solution, or with dilute H2SO4. 



In practice, a small amount of Co<sup>2+</sup> is extracted. The phenolic oxime acts like ammonia and exerts a strong ligand field favoring oxidation to Co<sup>3+</sup> . Co<sup>3+</sup> can only be removed from the organic by reductive stripping in acid with a reducing metal such as Zn or Fe, which converts inert Co<sup>3+</sup> to labile Co<sup>2+</sup> (Eqn. 9). An unavoidable consequence of this treatment is that a significant amount of the oxime is degraded to ketone by the aggressive conditions of the reductive strip, so re-oximation is necessary before the organic can be returned to the circuit. 



The Yabulu refinery in Townsville, Queensland, operates an ammoniacal SX circuit with ketoxime, and the Co level in the organic is maintained at < 3 g/L by treating a bleed stream to remove Co<sup>(25)</sup> . At this level of Co loading, 0.15 mol/L of ketoxime is coordinated to Co<sup>3+</sup> assuming a 3:1 stoichiometry, poisoning 30% of the ketoxime reagent (typical concentration is 15% v/v). 

Other limitations of phenolic oximes in ammoniacal media include slow extraction and stripping kinetics for Ni, slow phase separation, and Cu build up. The strong ammonia strip that recovers Ni does not fully recover Cu, so a bleed stream of the organic must be treated with H2SO4 to prevent accumulation of Cu on the organic<sup>(23)</sup> . 

###### **Basic Extractants** 

###### **_Amine Reagents_** 

There are four types of amine reagents, primary (RNH2), secondary (R2NH), tertiary (R3N) and quaternary (R4N<sup>+</sup> ), although only tertiary amines are used in Ni laterite processing. Separation of Ni and Co from chloride media using tertiary amines operates by an entirely different mechanism to 

197 

the acidic extractants. In chloride solution, Co<sup>2+</sup> readily forms a variety of chloride complexes, and at sufficiently high chloride concentrations, the tetrahedral anionic complex [CoCl4]<sup>2-</sup> is dominant. Conversely, Ni<sup>2+</sup> does not easily form anionic chloride complexes in HCl solution (although [NiCl4]<sup>2-</sup> can form in aqueous Me4NCl<sup>(27)</sup> and saturated LiCl solution<sup>(5)</sup> ). 

Ni extraction from chloride solutions using a tertiary amine has been reported<sup>(28)</sup> , but

high extraction (>80%) was only possible from solutions containing >7 g/L Ni, > 3 mol/L HCl using >50% v/v amine in xylene. In 5 mol/kg HCl solution, with 1 mol/kg Ni (~60 g/L Ni), the dominant species is Ni<sup>2+</sup> aq<sup>,</sup> with about 20% present as NiCl<sup>+</sup> aq<sup>, and at 1 mol/kg HCl, the fraction of NiCl+</sup> aq<sup>does not exceed 10%</sup> in the range 0.01-1.0 mol/kg Ni<sup>(29)</sup> . Therefore, at low pH, the tertiary amine is protonated (R3NH<sup>+</sup> ) and two such ammonium cations form an ion pair with [CoCl4]<sup>2-</sup> , selectively extracting Co into the organic phase (Eqn. 10), while Ni remains in the raffinate<sup>(10)</sup> . 



As mentioned earlier, tertiary amines are utilized in the Goro flowsheet to separate Co and Ni from the CYANEX 301 strip solution. The Ni-HCl solution is subjected to pyrohydrolysis to recover NiO and HCl<sup>(19)</sup> . The use of chloride media and amine extractants creates a corrosive environment requiring special materials of construction. Slow phase disengagement is also of concern, requiring the use of an all-aromatic (and consequently low flash point) diluent to maintain low viscosity and minimize aqueous in organic entrainment<sup>(23)</sup> . 

###### **RESEARCH DEVELOPMENTS AND IMPLICATIONS** 

###### **Synergistic SX** 

Flett<sup>(30)</sup> was the first to demonstrate a synergistic effect on metal extraction between an aliphatic α- hydroxyoxime and a carboxylic acid. In the following decades, extensive research on the application of synergistic mixtures applied to Ni/Co separation in the context of Ni laterite exploitation has been carried out, most recently by CSIRO researchers<sup>(31)</sup> . The most promising combination consists of an aliphatic α-hydroxy oxime, a carboxylic acid and tributyl phosphate (TBP). This synergistic mixture possesses good selectivity against Mn, Mg and Ca and extracts Ni and Co in the pH 5-6 range. The extracted Ni complex consists of two oximes and two carboxylates, and TBP is essential to achieve sufficiently rapid Ni extraction and stripping kinetics. Another approach has been to exploit this kinetic difference to separate Co from Ni in extraction and stripping<sup>(32)(33)</sup> , although in general kinetic separations are more difficult to control in real processes than thermodynamic ones. 

The major drawback of this approach is the instability of the oxime, which is susceptible to hydrolysis and oxidation (Figure 6), both under acidic stripping conditions (forming acyloin and diketone)<sup>(34)</sup> and metal-loaded extraction conditions (forming diketone and keto-oxime)<sup>(35)</sup> . It is particularly vulnerable to upset conditions resulting in high Mn loading which leads to more rapid degradation<sup>(36)</sup> . Keto-oxime formation is also promoted by Co extraction. Acyloin formation is reversible via re-oximation, and while reduction of the keto-oxime back to the hydroxyoxime is technically possible with sodium b

orohydride (but not with metallic Zn or Fe)<sup>(37)</sup> , the cost of this treatment would be quite high.

###### **Pre-loaded Carboxylate SX** 

Ni and Co extraction from laterite PLS using a Mg-loaded carboxylic acid was recently proposed<sup>(38)</sup> . According to this patent application, the Mg-loaded carboxylic acid extracts Ni, Co, Zn, Cu and Mn from the laterite PLS after first removing Fe. The loaded organic is then contacted with a concentrated NiCl2 solution, which scrubs Co, Mn, Zn, Cu, Mg and Ca. Ni is stripped with sulfuric acid and recovered by electrowinning or another technique. Co and Mn are subsequently extracted away from Zn, Cu, Mg and Ca using another SX circuit (containing an amine extractant), and Co is selectively precipitated as a sulfide from the strip solution. This process has been considered for the Agata project in the Philippines<sup>(39)</sup> . 

While the reagent is low cost, the flowsheet is complicated, containing numerous scrubbing and washing stages as well as Mg-loading stages. Furthermore, the use of different extractants (carboxylic acid and amine) runs the risk of reagent cross-contamination. 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

Solvent extraction continues to have an important role in the Ni laterite industry, with Murrin Murrin in operation since 1996, the SX portion of the Yabulu refinery operating since 1989 and Ambatovy and Goro due to become fully operational in 2012. Both Murrin Murrin and Ambatovy separate Ni from Co using phosphinic acid SX after first rejecting Mg, Ca and Mn via sulfide precipitation. Metallic Ni and Co are then recovered from the purified solutions by H2 reduction. The Yabulu refinery treats a variety of feedstocks by leaching with ammonia, oxidizing Co<sup>2+</sup> to Co<sup>3+</sup> , extracting Ni and producing high purity Ni metal, carbonate and oxide, and mixed Co oxide/carbonate. The Goro plant will reject the impurities Mn, Mg and Ca by extracting Ni and Co directly from the PLS with CYANEX 301, and then separate Co from Ni by extraction with a tertiary amine from the HCl strip solution, producing Co carbonate and Ni oxide. 

Despite the range of available reagents and flowsheets, none possess the ideal combination of high selectivity for Ni and Co against Mn, Mg and Ca and high resistance to chemical degradation. The development of an SX route that avoids precipitation and does not require special measures to minimize degradation would simplify flowsheets, improve recovery and produce higher quality, higher value products. Ideally, such a reagent would recover and separate Ni and Co simultaneously from the major impurities that are present in large amounts in high concentration in laterite PLS (Mn, Mg and Ca). Development continues by the major players to balance the compromises and provide a solution to the clear need for a more selective and robust extractant for the Ni laterite industry.

###### **RECOVERY OF

COPPER FROM STRONG CHLORIDE SOLUTIONS BY SOLVENT EXTRACTION** 

By 

Zhaowu Zhu & Chu Yong Cheng 

CSIRO Process Science and Engineering CSIRO Minerals Down Under National Research Flagship, Australia, 

Presenter and Corresponding Author 

###### **Chu Yong Cheng** 

chu.cheng@csiro.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

A new mixed solvent extraction system consisting of LIX 63, LIX 860 and TBP was developed to extract and transfer copper from strong chloride solutions to sulphate solutions for conventional electrowinning. Copper is separated from other base metals such as iron, nickel, zinc, etc. in extraction. The co-extracted impurities are removed with reasonably strong chloride solution by scrubbing. The chloride in the impurity-removed organic solution is scrubbed with weak chloride solution. Copper is readily stripped from the scrubbed organic solution to generate copper electrolyte containing very small amount of chloride (36 mg/L) and iron (5 mg/L) suitable for electrowinning. Further research work is required to optimise the organic system and the iron and chloride scrubbing steps. 

Based on the new mixed solvent extraction system, a conceptual process flowsheet has been proposed with the advantages of: 

- Copper can be transferred from chloride to sulphate solution with one solvent extraction circuit. 

- No expensive base is required for copper extraction and transfer to sulphate solution for electrowinning. 

- Iron, other base metals and chloride can be scrubbed from the loaded organic solution. 

- Copper can be readily stripped to recycle the organic solution and generate suitable electrolyte for electrowinning. 

203 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

In order to overcome the drawbacks of high energy consumption and high environmental concerns of pyrometallurgy to treat copper sulphide ores, a number of hydrometallurgy processes have been developed (Schweitzer and Livingston, 1982; Mukherjee, et al., 1985; Szymanowski, 1996; Flett, 2002; Senanayake and Muir, 2003; Peacey, et al., 2004; Hyvдrinen and Hдmдlдinen, 2005; Lundstrom, et al., 2005; Harris, et al., 2006 and 2007; Velбsquez-Yйvenes, et al., 2010). Among them the chloride-based processes attract much attention due to the advantages of high metal recovery, fast leaching kinetics, effective precious metal recovery, low waste discharge and, therefore, low environmental pollution. For copper recovery from secondary sources, a chloridebased process plays a critical role (Oishi, et al., 2007; Masvetas, et al., 2009). One of the hurdles to impede the application of chloride processing is that conventional electrowinning cannot be used for the recovery of copper from chloride solutions. Copper electrowinning from chloride solutions generates harmful chlorine gas and a non-ideal copper powder product and needs specially designed expensive cells. 

The use of solvent extraction to extract copper from chloride solution and transfer it to sulphate solution has been reported by a number of researcher

s using different reagents (Kyuchoukov and Mihaylov, 1991; Fletcher et al., 1991; Cierpiszewski and Szymanowski, 2001). Recently, the use of LIX 63 and Versatic 10 was reported to successfully transfer copper from chloride solutions to sulphate solution at pH 3-4 (Cheng et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2012). However, compared with conventional copper solvent extraction using chelating reagents in sulphate solutions such as LIX 984 and Acorga M5640, expensive base has to be used for the adjustment of solution pH to keep the copper in the organic solution during chloride scrubbing, resulting in extra operating costs. To overcome this problem, a new mixed organic system consisting of LIX 63 and LIX 860 has been developed to extract copper in a strong chloride solution and transfer it to a sulphate solution without neutralisation using base for its recovery by conventional electrowinning. ###### **COPPER EXTRACTION FROM CHLORIDE SOLUTIONS WITH LIX 63 AND LIX 860** Copper was extracted and separated from Fe(III) in aqueous solutions containing 300 g/L CaCl2 and various HCl concentrations using different combinations of LIX 63 and LIX 860 concentrations with a total concentration of LIX 63 and LIX 860 being 0.4 M in Shellsol D70 under A/O ratio of 1:1 at 40 °C (Fig. 1). Copper was extracted effectively by the 0.4 M LIX 63 alone system with about 95% Cu extraction in the HCl concentration range of 0 – 0.5 M after a single contact. This means that the copper extraction by LIX63 in strong chloride solutions is independent of solution acidity, indicating a solvating mechanism reported by Szymanowski (1996) and described in a previous paper with another mixed organic system of LIX 63 and Versatic 10 (Zhu et al. 2011). The reaction of copper extraction from strong chloride solutions by LIX 63 is presented in Equation 1 (Sato et al., 1987). With the decrease of LIX 63 concentration in the mixed organic solutions, the copper extraction decreased gradually and reached the lowest value with the 0.4 M LIX 860 alone system. With this system, the increase in the HCl concentration from 0 to 0.5 M resulted in decrease in copper extraction significantly from about 68% to 6%. This means that the copper extraction by LIX 860 in strong chloride solutions depends on solution acidity, indicating that LIX 860 deprotonates to effect metal extraction. The reaction of copper extraction from strong chloride solutions by LIX 860 is presented in Equation 2. where LH represents LIX 860. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Development of Outotec VSF<sup>®</sup> technology dates back to the 1970’s, the first commercial application being Kokkola Mo SX Plant in Finland (1977). Zaldнvar in Chile was the first Cu SX plant to utilize the technology (1995), which has gone through several versions and incremental improvements from the first projects to the most recent. The latest projects are retrofit project of Chuquicamata Oxide Plant Train A (start-up in 2008), Franke Cu SX-EW (2009), Assarel Cu SX-EW (2010), Tia Marнa Cu SX-EW (start-up date unknown), Caserones Cu SX-EW (2012), a confidential U SX project (2012) and a confidential Co/Ni SX project (after 2015). 

The objective of this paper is to discuss the experiences of the Chuquicamata and Franke projects and specifically the results of technological improvements implemented in them. The Chuquicamata retrofit project was the first of its kind executed by Outotec, with incorporation of VSF technology in an existing, operative solvent extraction train to increase its PLS processing capacity. Downtime required for the installation of VSF equipment was minimized by incorporation of by-pass pipelines to the separate stages and installing the VSF equipment stage by stage, keeping the train in operation during the whole intervention sequence. In the Franke Project, a new concept of combined Washing stage and Loaded Organic tank was utilized for the first time, providing approximately 15% CAPEX reduction for the SX plant. Additionally, Outotec<sup>®</sup> Reverse settler design was utilised in order to further optimize the plant layout in terms of operational ergonomics. 

213 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The existing VSF<sup>®</sup> (Vertical Smooth Flow) solvent extraction plants account for about 30% of the total world-wide copper solvent extraction capacity<sup>(1, 2)</sup> and about 15% of the global cobalt solvent extraction capacity<sup>(3)</sup> . 

VSF technology includes three main equipment units: 

- DOP<sup>®</sup> (Dispersion Overflow Pump) pumping unit, 

- SPIROK<sup>®</sup> mixing unit, 

- Outotec<sup>®</sup> Compact or Reverse settler with DDG<sup>®</sup> (Dispersion Depletor Gate) fences 

Principal distinctive features of VSF technology are: 

- Separated pumping and mixing 

- Low head overall design resulting in low tip speeds of the DOP pumps 

- Mixing with the helicoidal SPIROK agitators, which create a vertical flow pattern in the mixer tanks 

- Compact, deep settler design with DD

G fences and high settling rates 

One of the beneficial characteristics of the overall VSF design is that the generated dispersion has narrower droplet size distribution and larger average droplet size, when compared to conventional SX plant design. This has been demonstrated by droplet size measurements made in industrial plant conditions. Some measurement results are shown in Figures 1 and 2.

The operating principle of DDG<sup>®</sup> fences has not been extensively discussed in the earlier publications made by Outotec<sup>(5, 6)</sup> , so that the principle and operating features of the DDG fences are described briefly here. A schematic illustration of DDG fence operation is shown in Figure 3. 

214 



**Figure 3: DDG Fence Operation (Side View)** 

Dispersion flowing towards the discharge end of the settler is accumulated behind the first, solid plate of the DDG fence (on the left hand side in Figure 1) and is forced to flow under the first plate and over the second plate, through a vertical slot in between the plates. Due to this structure, DDG fences distribute the dispersion flow efficiently along 



**Figure 4: CFD Model Velocity Profile for Outotec**<sup>**®**</sup> **Reverse Settler Feed Side with DDG Fences** 

the width of the settler, even though their principal duty is to enhance phase separation and removal of fine droplets from the continuous phase. In addition to the operating DDG<sup>®</sup> fence installations, this distributing influence can be observed also in one-phase CFD models made by Outotec. An example of the results of a simulation made for Outotec<sup>®</sup> Reverse settler is shown in Figure 4. 

Dispersion accumulated upstream of the fence acts as a “filter” for the small droplets of discontinuous phase, enhancing their coalescence. Separated organic phase gets to flow over the DDG fence through a slotted section of the first plate and the same principle is applied for the separated aqueous flow below the fence. In this way the pressure drop of the fence can be minimized, which contributes to the overall low-head design of a VSF plant. 

DDG fences and Outotec settler design have also been optimized to tolerate conditions, where gypsum precipitation or very high PLS solids loading may occur. It has been demonstrated at Outotec reference plants, that the deep settler design provides more flexibility to tolerate such extreme conditions, as may be seen in the Picture 1. At this plant the PLS solids and calcium concentrations have consistently been well above the maximum operational limits. However, it has been possible to operate the plant with normal flows during prolonged periods.

Outotec VSF<sup>®</sup> technology has been developed in several steps from the first projects to the latest, which are the VSF retrofit project of Codelco´s Chuquicamata Oxide Plant Train A (start-up in 2008), Quadra Mining´s Franke Project (2009), Assarel (2010), Southern Perъ Copper Corporation’s Tia Marнa (start-up date unknown), Minera Lumina Copper’s Caserones (2012), a confidential U SX project (2012) and a confidential Co/Ni SX project (after 2015). The objective of this paper is to discuss the experiences of Chuquicamata and Franke projects and specifically the results of technological developments implemented in them. 

###### **METHODOLOGY** 

Information presented in this paper has been collected from Outotec’s internal reports, engineering documents in the reviewed projects, operational data of actual operations received from the plant operators and public external sources. 

CFD modelling reviewed in this paper has been made with FLUENT 6.3 software. 

O/A entrainments discussed in this paper (Chuquicamata project) were analyzed with Horiba analyzer using the Horiba standard method. A/O entrainments were measured with “Chuquicamatatype minicoalescer”, which is used at several SX plants in Chile. 

###### **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION** 

###### **Chuquicamata Retrofit Project** 

Codelco’s Chuquicamata Oxide Plant Train A was converted from conventional to VSF<sup>®</sup> technology in 2008. ###### **CENTRIFUGATION SOLUTION FOR CRUD TREATMENT IN HYDOMETALLURGY PROCESSES** 

By

###### **ABSTRACT** 

In the hydrometal process, the presence of the so-called “crud” is a constant challenge in solvent extraction. Crud is a stable emulsion which forms along the interface between the aqueous and organic phase. The spread is influenced by the following parameters: first, wind blows the dust and impurities into the open sedimentation tanks. Second, the undissolved solids such as sa

nd transported in the PLS cause problems in conjunction with incorrect agitator design. 

The crud fraction can decisively impact the efficiency of the hydrometal extraction because the phase interface can constitute a large fraction and the sedimentation tanks cannot react flexibly to it. In the downstream process of the series-connected sedimentation tanks, they are thus all contaminated with crud. At the same time, the necessary mass transport is significantly impeded at the phase boundary between organic phase and aqueous phase due to the crud formation. 

The transfer of the organic phase into the electrolysis cell can result in a “burnout” of the cathode. The carry-over of this electrolyte into the extraction can cause problems with the pH regulation. The carry-over of the organic components into the raffinate also leads to contamination of the leaching circuit. 

The continuous treatment of the crud with a 3-phase decanter centrifuge is extremely effective in combating this. This technology splits all three phases from each other and they are consequently continuously separated. All subsequent process steps exhibit a stable, uniform effectiveness. The main advantage for the user is that fluctuations in the process are eliminated and the organic phase can be recirculated back to extraction. The recycling of the solvent alone justifies the investment in less than 6 months as examples from South Africa and Chile show. 

To operate solvent recovery in daily operation fully automated online at the optimum limit, the decanter centrifuge is equipped with a concentration-dependent pond adjustment called DControl®. By this means, the users can be guaranteed the maximum possible solvent recovery and minimise the solvent costs in this process step. This system is presented in detail in this paper. 

221 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The number of applications for continuous centrifugation in the hydrometal process is rising continuously. This development is characterized by a number of clear user demands in which decanters are clearly superior to other competing technologies. 

This user demand relating to productivity, process specifications, reliability and profitability can be achieved and even surpassed. The demands of different production facilities involved in the hydrometal process always vary because the respective composition of the ore requires a unique process sequence. Consequently, application-specific demands are realized in close cooperation with the user. Preventive service concepts are a basic pre-condition for constant plant availability which ensures the user the leading position in hydrometallurgy.

###### **FLOTATION OF OXIDE COPPER ORES: A REVIEW FROM LABORATORY TESTING TO INDUSTRIAL PRACTICE** 

By 

Graeme Sheldon 

AMML Pty Ltd, Australia 

Presenter and Corresponding Author 

**Graeme Sheldon** Graeme.Sheldon@tpg.com.au 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Flotation has been used for many years as a method for recovering and upgrading oxide copper minerals into mineral concentrates. The traditional approach has been based on sulphidisation of the oxide copper minerals surfaces followed by collector to render these surfaces hydrophobic. Sulphidisation processes usually are very effective and efficient at laboratory scale, however are more problematic at industrial scale leading to inferior plant performance compared to laboratory performance. In more recent times, the use of hydroxamate collectors has been demonstrated to be effective at both laboratory and industrial scale for oxide copper mineral flotation, and commercial quantities of hydroxamates are now available for commercial use. 

(Note: Author unable to attend the Conference) 

231 

###### **SELECTION OF THE PROCESS: FLOTATION VERSUS LEACHING** 

Why float oxide copper ores when oxide copper minerals leach so well? Oxide copper ores generally respond very well to acid leaching (e.g. heap leaching followed by SX/EW). However, there are situations where grinding and flotation may be the preferred process route. These situations include: 

- Ores containing significant quantities of carbonates or other alkali rock minerals can be large acid consumers; hence the economics of acid leaching can be prohibitive. Flotation becomes a potential alternative process where the alkaline nature of the ore can be an advantage, negating the need for lime additions to maintain a slightly alkaline pH in the flotation pulps. 

- Ore deposits that contain some oxide ore with a larger sulphide ore type component. The larger sulphide component would tend to dictate the processing route, and conventionally copper sulphides are recovered to saleable mineral concentrates by grinding and flotation. Hence, treatment of the oxide ore component would be considered utilising the planned or existing flotation plant, rather than committing funding to a leaching and metal recovery process for a limited ore supply. 

- Transition and supergene ores containing a mix of sulphide and oxide copper minerals. Direct leaching of these ores would be expected to recover copper from the oxide minerals, however secondary sulphide minerals (e.g. bornite and chalcocite) and primary sulphides (e.g. chalcopyrite) would have limited solubility by direct acid leaching, hence giving limited o

verall recovery from these ore types. Flotation can be successful at recovering the sulphide and oxide copper minerals in separate sequential sulphide then oxide flotation stages. With recent industrial developments in oxide flotation the sulphide and oxide copper minerals can be floated simultaneously into a single concentrate. 

Hence, the process selection for the treatment of ores containing oxide copper minerals would include 

- Consideration of the presence of alkaline minerals that would consume acid 

- The quantity of oxide ore for treatment 

- The availability of process equipment (e.g. a flotation plant or SX/EW plant) 

- Any presence of sulphide copper minerals with the oxide minerals, and liberation locking mineralogy of the minerals which could affect the flotation performance. 

###### **OXIDE COPPER MINERAL FLOTATION TECHNOLOGIES** 

While there are several reagent systems that have been used in laboratory studies, only two are currently commonly used commercially. These are: 

- Sulphidisation of the oxide copper mineral surface using S<sup>2-</sup> ion (from NaHS or Na2S), followed by a collector such as xanthate. 

- Direct flotation after addition of a hydroxamate collector. 

Other processes have included carboxylic acids, amines, and anionic collectors; however these are less common practices in modern flotation operations. 

###### **Sulphidisation** 

Sulphidisation has been practiced commercially for many years. The process usually works very well in laboratory scale, however can be quite troublesome to operate in an industrial plant which often results in lower concentrate copper grades and recoveries than achieved at laboratory scale. The process involves the addition of solutions of either NaHS or Na2S, with the S<sup>2-</sup> ion reacting with the Cu on the mineral surfaces to form unstable copper sulphide on the oxide copper mineral surface<sup>(1)</sup> . When collector (e.g. xanthate) is added, it reacts with sulphide surface layer on the oxide minerals forming a hydrophobic surface and hence the mineral is amenable to flotation. The sulphide layer on the mineral surface is unstable, and multiple additions (typically from 3 to 10 addition points) of NaHS during flotation are required to maintain the sulphide surfaces and maximise copper recovery to concentrates. 

There are two main methods of achieving sulphidisation. 

232 

One is by a manual dose of NaHS or Na2S using a trial and error approach and visual assessment of the resulting froth to gauge whether the dose should be increased or decreased etc. In an industrial plant this would normally involve continuous additions to conditioners with manual adjustment of the dose. The effect of excess addition is an excess of S<sup>2-</sup> in solution causing copper mineral depression. As the S<sup>2-</sup> oxidises rapidly (particularly in the aerated flotation cells) the depressive conditions reduce until sulphidised copper minerals are seen to float in cells fur

ther down the flotation bank. There is a tendency to over add the sulphidiser, and allow aeration in the flotation cells to reduce the residual S<sup>2-</sup> until the right conditions are achieved to allow flotation. However continued oxidation of S<sup>2-</sup> leads to under sulphidised conditions, and lower Cu flotation rates and recovery, and hence multiple NaHS addition stages are required. Using this “hit and miss” manual approach, the result is generally excessive NaHS additions and less than optimum flotation performance and copper mineral recovery. 

The second method of achieving sulphidisation is a more scientific approach. The process is called controlled potential sulphidisation (CPS). It is based on additions of a sulphidiser (e.g. NaHS) to a measured and controlled residual of S<sup>2-</sup> in solution. This is measured using a sulphide ion selective and reference electrode couple in laboratory scale work. The ion selective electrodes are not normally used in industrial plants as the electrodes deteriorate relatively quickly and require very regular maintenance. For industrial measurements, a less precise method uses a platinum Redox electrode couple, which is more robust. As a guide, the Es would normally be controlled to about - 500mV to -600mV with an ion selective electrode and reference couple, compared to an EPt (mV not converted to the hydrogen electrode) of about -230mV to -260mV using the platinum and reference electrode couple. 

Sulphidisation is effective for the flotation of the main oxide copper minerals of economic interest, including: 

• Malachite Cu2(OH)CO3 • Azurite Cu3(OH)2(CO3)2 • Cuprite Cu2O • Tenorite CuO 

However sulphidisation is not effective for flotation of chrysocolla: CuO. SiO2 

In the case of treatment of an ore containing both sulphide and oxide copper minerals, it is normal to recover the sulphide minerals first with sulphide collectors, and then treat the sulphide flotation tailing with a sulphidiser (NaHS or Na2S) and collector, in multiple stages for oxide copper flotation. If cleaning is required to achieve saleable grade concentrates it would also normally be completed in separate cleaner flotation circuits for the sulphides and oxides. The need for separate circuits is due to the sulphidiser being a depressant for sulphide copper minerals, and hence attempts at sulphidisation of oxide copper minerals in the presence of sulphide copper minerals usually results in poor recovery of the sulphide copper minerals. 

###### **Hydroxamate Collectors** 

Hydroxamates for direct flotation of oxide copper minerals is not new technology. Patents were awarded in the 1940’s and there has been regular research activity since<sup>(2)</sup> , however the work had been limited to laboratory work only. However in recent years Ausmelt Limited, based in Melbourne, proceeded to commercialise the manufacture of alkyl hydroxamates for oxide base metal recovery, and they pursued years of commercial development w

ork including plant trials, commercial sales and technical assistance. 

Flotation of oxide copper minerals with hydroxamates is relatively robust, although not without its difficulties. The process has many similarities to simple sulphide flotation, where the collector is added, conditioned and flotation commenced. The collector bonds directly with the oxide copper minerals, without the need for any sulphidisation or other chemical activators. The hydroxamates are effective over a reasonably wide pH range of generally pH 7 to pH 10.5. The flotation process is relatively stable and usually less addition stages are needed compared to sulphidisation. Other collectors such as xanthate are not normally necessary for flotation of oxide copper minerals only. 

As flotation of oxide copper minerals with hydroxamates does not require sulphidisation, there is no depressive effect on any copper sulphides. Hydroxamates have minimal or no significant effect on copper sulphides. Hence, hydroxamates allow for flotation of sulphides and oxides simultaneously 

233 

by using a copper sulphide collector (e.g. xanthate) and the hydroxamate copper oxide collector into the same conditioners or flotation stages. This had been demonstrated at laboratory and industrial scale. At the Fox Resources Radio Hill operations, the addition of a hydroxamate called AM28 (at the time supplied by Ausmelt Limited) increased total copper recoveries by up to 20% when used in conjunction with sulphide collectors for the treatment of supergene ore<sup>(3)</sup> . The ore contained primary and secondary sulphide copper minerals with lesser quantities of cuprite, malachite and azurite. 

In a laboratory test program, primary sulphide and oxide copper ores from the Minto Mine in Canada was blended and used for flotation studies<sup>(2)</sup> . The ore contained 39% of the total copper as acid soluble (oxide) copper. The main minerals present in the blended ore were chalcocite, chalcopyrite, bornite, malachite, and minor azurite. Using a combination of hydroxamate and sulphide collectors, the sulphide and oxide minerals were floated together at the same time with high recoveries (95.5%), and after one stage of cleaning the concentrate graded 33.4% Cu. The tests were supported with chemical analysis and QEMSCAN mineralogical evaluations. A test with sulphidisation on the same blend demonstrated the sulphides were depressed when it was attempted to float the sulphides and oxides together with sulphidisation and sulphide collectors only. 

Hydroxamates have been demonstrated to be effective for the recovery of the same minerals as for sulphidisation, as well as chrysocolla<sup>(4)</sup> . 

###### **ORE RELATED FACTORS THAT CAN AFFECT OXIDE COPPER FLOTATION PERFORMANCE** 

Ores containing oxide copper minerals usually contain other oxidised and weathered minerals. These can contribute to flotation difficulties and or limit flotation performance and copper recovery. Oxide ores often contain h

igh contents of slimes, clays and goethite. Slimes and clays can cause problems with excessive entrainment in the froth, diluting copper grades in the concentrates and contributing to strong and stable froths. Slimes and clays can foul the oxide copper mineral surfaces by the formations of thin films of slimes gangue. These negative effects can usually be reduced by additions of dispersants and froth modifiers to aid in the dispersion of the slimes. Dispersants such as sodium silicate, and depressants such as starch, dextrin, lignin sulphonate, quebracho and cellulose type products can be effective. Any fouled surfaces of copper minerals can be cleaned using attritioning and or high intensity conditioning. The effects can be quite dramatic. Figure 1 shows the effect of high intensity conditioning on copper recovery for an oxide ore containing malachite and azurite and a high content of slimes and clays, from Morocco. Hydroxamates were used for copper flotation. The rougher concentrate grades from all the tests were similar, at >20% Cu. Test conditions were identical except for the intensity of the conditioning. ISADVANATAGES OF SULPHIDISATION AND HYDROXAMATES FOR OXIDE COPPER MINERAL FLOTATION** CPS flotation at laboratory scale is very efficient; works very well, uses the optimum dose of sulphidiser and achieves optimum flotation performance. However, industrially, CPS is difficult and many operations (if not all) eventually abandon the process and revert to simple manual dosing, or some form of hybrid (an attempt at some control), with less than optimum addition of the sulphidiser, and incomplete or excessive (or both) sulphidisation. The industrial process problems with CPS relate to the unstable and very fast reactions of sulphidiser in mineral slurries combined with the longer conditioning and flotation residence times, and the lower power input via agitators (both conditioners and flotation cells) per tonne of ore or slurry compared to laboratory flotation tests. Compared to 3 litre laboratory conditioner volumes with strong agitation and high power input per litre of slurry the plant conditioners can be several thousands of litres, usually with a single agitator operated as efficiently as possible with the least power draw required to keep the pulp in suspension, producing slowly stirred slurry. The sulphidiser is usually added to a single point in the conditioner. The sulphidiser is not quickly and evenly distributed, and the pulp zones in the conditioner away from the sulphidiser are under sulphidised, while those near the sulphidiser addition point are strongly over sulphidised. Hand held Eh or Es measurements at different zones around the surface of the conditioner usually give substantial differences in mV reading, demonstrating the inhomogeneous conditioning. 235 This inhomogeneous sulphidisation produces sub optimum flotation and copper recovery, and is a major cause for the performance difference between laboratory tests and industrial operations. The conditioning issues of sulphidiser and subsequent inferior flotation performance (compared to laboratory tests) is a significant disadvantage compared to hydroxamates. Hydroxamates are added to the pulp in a similar way to additions of collector for sulphide flotation. Hydroxamates are best added to a conditioner, however there is less importance for fast and homogenous agitation, and the reactions of hydroxamates with the pulp are much less severe and appear to be much slower than sulphidisers. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Froth flotation is a method used to separate the desired mineral particles from the associated gangue mineral based on the differences in their hydrophobicity. It is used to treat nickel sulphide ores containing pyrrhotite, pentlandite and magnesium oxide. The Collectors are the reagents used in the froth flotation to impart the hydrophobicity to the desired mineral. 

Potassium amyl xanthate (PAX) is one of the preferred collectors used in froth flotation of nickel sulphide ores. The xanthate collectors are sensitive to pH and their selectivity in treating complex ores is questionable. With deteriorating nickel sulphide ore reserves more selective collectors have to be used in the extraction of nickel. The dithiophosphates are believed to be more selective than xanthates but cost more. 

The addition of a second collector in the froth flotation system improves surface coverage which is promoted by the collector co-adsorption. The synergistic effects or linear summation of constituents’ adsorption characteristics may improve the overall flotation performance with regard to recovery and grade. 

PAX was mixed with either sodium di-methyl dithiocarbamate (di-C1-DTC) or sodium di-ethyl dithiophosphate (di-C2-DTP) to investigate whether there were any improvements in recoveries and grades compared to pure xan

thate collectors. The following mixtures were tested in this work 

90% PAX and 10% di-C1-DTC; 90% PAX and 10% di-C2-DTP; 70% PAX and 30% di-C1-DTC; and 70% PAX and 30% di-C2-DTP 

This study showed that the mixture 90% PAX and 10% di-C1-DTC yielded higher nickel recovery and nickel grade than the pure PAX. It was not beneficial to use both mixtures of PAX with di-C2DTP. The nickel recoveries and nickel grades obtained with the use of these mixtures were lower than those obtained with pure PAX.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Nickel sulphide mineral ores amount to more than fifty percent of all commercial nickel<sup>(24)</sup> . There is a growing demand for nickel and it is projected that the current nickel sulphide reserves may be depleted by 2030<sup>(24)</sup> . The nickel sulphide ore reserves are declining and are mostly of low nickel grade. Consequently, more selective methods should be used in their beneficiation. Pyrrhotite and magnesium oxide are the primary gangue in nickel sulphide floatation. High smelting costs are associated with magnesium oxide while high sulphur dioxide emissions are caused by the high levels of pyrrhotite in the nickel sulphide flotation concentrates. The nickel sulphide processing industry needs to be more efficient and cost effective to be sustainable as it faces the following challenges<sup>(20)</sup> : 

1. The growing demand for nickel 

2. The deteriorating nickel prices 

3. The strict environmental constraints especially on sulphur emissions 

4. The challenge posed by nickel oxide ores as primary source of nickel 

The xanthates are the cheapest and the most abundant class of thiol collectors. The xanthate collectors are generally strong collectors and least selective compared to the other thiol collectors. This may be problematic when grades becomes lower and lower; as the xanthates may not be able to efficiently concentrate the complex and low grade ores<sup>(24)</sup> . Sodium ethyl xanthate (SEX) and potassium amyl xanthate (PAX) are the common collectors used in the selective froth flotation of nickel sulphide mineral ores. However, they are not sufficiently selective in the flotation of complex sulphide ores<sup>(16)</sup> . Sodium di-ethyl-dithiophosphates (di-C2-DTP) and sodium di-methyldithiocarbamates (di-C1-DTC) may replace the xanthates as they are more selective to sulphide minerals<sup>(14)</sup> . However, it is not economically feasible to use each of them alone due to their higher cost compared to the xanthates. The literature provided enough evidence of the benefits associated with the use of the collector mixtures over pure collectors, and the present study explored the feasibility of using PAX and its mixtures on the flotation of the nickel sulphide mineral ore. The addition of a second collector to a froth flotation system may alter the adsorption characteristics of each of the collectors on a sulphide mineral surface<sup>(22)</sup>

.This may result in enhanced grade and recovery due to either synergistic effects or linear summation of constituents’ absorption characteristics<sup>(4)</sup> . The coverage of the mineral surface may also be improved due to collector constituents’ co-adsorption on the mineral surface<sup>10)</sup> . 

The mixtures of collectors may be able to reduce the collector dosage requirements without the loss of selectivity. In such instances, the collector-mixtures usage serve a dual purpose i.e. cost saving and performance improvement. Hence, the use of collector mixtures is the most common alternative remedy to poor flotation grades and recoveries. The mixture of collectors can be easily manipulated to satisfy the need and can be used successfully for both bulk flotation and selective flotation. Pure collectors are ore-specific and a tiresome<sup>(</sup> amount of experiments is required to choose the most suitable collector for a particular mineral ore<sup>1)</sup> .There is no single collector that can be used in the selective flotation of all minerals in the ore; but a well designed mixture of collectors may cover a wider range of ores than the pure collectors<sup>(14)</sup> . 

There are some collectors which are thermodynamically unable to adsorb onto some minerals surfaces when used alone; however these collectors are able to co-adsorb to such surfaces when used in the mixture<sup>(23)</sup> .The mixtures of collectors are efficient at low dosages, which imply that there is a minimal metal-collector precipitation when mixtures are used<sup>(22)</sup> . A collector-mineral adsorption is a very sensitive process. Therefore, a small change in the either a mineral surface or a collector alkyl group can produce a significant difference in the overall performance of the flotation system. This is more prevalent when a single collector is used. This problem is often encountered when the feed grade deteriorates over time. The collector mixtures are able to effectively deal with the varying feed grade<sup>(1)</sup> .The flotation rates may also improve when the mixture of collectors are used. The mixtures of collectors produce more stable froths, because of their ability to prevent formation of the collector multi-layer<sup>(10)</sup> . The stable froths are important especially in the recovery of the coarse particles. The mixtures of collectors are able to improve the recovery of the coarse particles due their higher stable froths compared to single collectors<sup>(10)(14)(4)(15)(13)(25)(28)</sup> 

The present study investigated if there were improvements on the nickel grades and recoveries with the use of PAX and its mixtures compared to the use of pure PAX. The collector PAX was mixed with either di-C1-DTC or di-C2-DTP and the mixtures contained either 90% PAX or 70% PAX.

###### **_The effects of PAX and its Mixtures with 10 and 30 mol % di-C1-DTC on Flotation Nickel Grade and Recovery_** 

A plot of percentage cumulative nickel grade versus cumulative nickel recovery obtained by the use of PAX and its mixtures with di-C1-DTC showed that the mixture of 90% PAX//10% di-C1-DTC yielded a higher nickel grade than pure PAX. The mixture 70% PAX//30% di-C1-DTC yielded a lower percentage cumulative nickel grade and recovery than pure PAX (Fig. 1). 



**Figure 1: Percentage cumulative nickel grade vs. nickel recovery obtained with pure PAX and its mixture with di-C1-DTC at a dosage 0.488 mmol/ton and different collector constituents’ ratio** 

The collector mixtures may improve one of the following: the recoveries, the grades or both the grades and the recoveries. The constituents of the mixture determine the improvements of the recoveries. The constituents’ ratio in the mixture determines the improvements of the grades. The mixture of compatible constituents at their optimum ratio improves both grades and recoveries<sup>(5)</sup> . However, the use of some collector mixtures is unable to yield the improved recoveries or grades or Klimpel rate constant<sup>(27)</sup> . The mixing of two collectors results in a reduced electrostatic repulsion between their ionic heads. The reduced electrostatic repulsion results in reduced surface tensions between their ionic heads. One collector in the mixture reduces the surface tensions by surrounding the polar group of the second collector. As the surface tension is reduced there is an increased collector concentration at the collector interface. The rate of bubble rapture is a function of this interfacial collector concentration. At higher interface concentration there is a low rate of bubble rapture. These low bubble raptures ensure successful carriage of the attached particles over to the froth phase<sup>(26)</sup> .Thus, there is a higher recovery at a low bubble rapture rate than at a higher bubble rapture rate. 

Sodium di-ethyl-DTC was weaker and more selective than PAX<sup>(18)</sup> . Thus, di-C1-DTC may have adsorbed on to the stronger sites on the mineral surface thereby leaving the weaker sites for PAX<sup>(10)</sup> . This resulted in more mineralized surfaces and improved

Thus, the presence of both di-10% C1-DTC and 90% PAX in the mixture may have improved the selectivity and lowered the degree of entrainment respectively.

###### **_The Effects of PAX and its Mixtures with 10 and 30 mol % di-C2-DTP on Flotation Nickel Grade and Recovery._** 

A plot of cumulative nickel grade versus cumulative nickel recovery showed that the use of the mixture 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP yielded a higher nickel recovery than the use of pure PAX (Fig. 4). The use of this mixture however yielded a lower cumulative nickel grade than the use of pure PAX. 



**Figure 4: Percentage cumulative nickel grade vs. nickel recovery obtained with pure PAX and its mixture with di-C2-DTP at a dosage 0.488 mmol/ton and different collector constituents’ ratio** 

The use of the mixture 70% PAX//30% di-C2-DTP yielded a higher nickel grade than the nickel grade yielded by the use of the mixture 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP. The use of 70% PAX//30% diC2-DTP mix

ture however yielded a lower cumulative nickel recovery than the use of 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP. These results perfectly illistrated the relationship between recovery and grade in froth flotation i.e. recovery increase with decrease in concentrate grade. 

The mixture 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP improved the nickel recovery only (Fig. 4). This mixture had a higher Klimpel rate constant than pure PAX, hence more material floated when this mixture was used. The more material floated the higher the recovery. The cumulative nickel grade was not positively affected as pure PAX was abundant and had a higher selectivity than pure di-C2-DTP<sup>(18)</sup> . Thus, the mixture behaved as pure PAX (Fig. 5). The concentration of di-C2-DTP could was too low to have a significant contribution to the mixture’s selectivity and ultimately nickel grade. 

245 

The mixture 70% PAX//30% di-C2-DTP yielded a higher nickel grade than the mixture 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP (Fig. 4). This result supported the above statement about concentration of diC2-DTP being to low to significantly affect the nickel grade. As stated above PAX was stronger and abudant constituent than di-C2-DTP. Thus, at a higher di-C2-DTP concentration there was an increase in the amount of the weaker collector to ensure that the weaker collector adsorbs onto as many stronger active site as posible. This would ensure an increased level of co-adsorption. 

A plot of cumulative nickel-to-iron recovery ratio versus flotation time showed there was no significant difference on the selectivity between PAX and its mixtures with di-C2-DTP. However, mixture 70% PAX //30% di-C2-DTP yielded a slightly higher selectivity than pure PAX especially in the initial stages of flotation (Fig. 5). 



**Figure 5: Cumulative change in nickel to iron recovery ratio obtained with PAX collector and its mixture with di-C2-DTP at a dosage 0.488 mmol/ton and different collector constituents’ ratio** 

The use of the mixture 70% PAX//30% di-C2-DTP yielded a higher selectivity than the use of pure PAX in the first three concentrates (Fig. 5). Due to this higher selectivity, the mixture 70% PAX//30% di-C2-DTP yielded a higher nickel grade than pure PAX. This was borne out by the plot of the graph of cumulative nickel grade versus cumulative nickel grade (Fig. 4). This mixture yielded a higher cumulative nickel grade than pure PAX in the interval where the selectivity obtained by the use of the mixture was higher than that obtained by the use of pure PAX. There was a drop in selectivity from the fourth concentrate and consequently there was a drop in the nickel grade in the same interval. The observed drop in selectivity may be related to two factors: 

1. The depletion of nickel mineral in the flotation cell as the flotation time increases 

Selectivity is the ratio of nickel to iron in the concentrate. The concentration of nickel sulphide mineral in the flotation cell decreased as the flotation time increased. Thus the ratio of nickel to

iron became smaller as flotation progressed as there was depletion of nickel in the flotation cell 

2.  Iron sulphide may have started floating as the flotation progresses. 

246 

Both the mixture PAX//di-C2-DTP increased the flotation rate of the poor floating minerals. Consequently, there was a shift in peak selectivity for these mixtures. Both the mixtures reached their highest selectivities faster than PAX (Fig. 5). Pure PAX obtained its highest selectivity in the fourth concentrate while the mixtures obtained theirs in the second concentrate. The increased flotation rate of slow floating mineral was not limited to valuable mineral as the gangue mineral also started floating. Consequently there was a loss of selectivity as the slow floating gangue minerals started floating as well. 

###### **_The Effects of PAX and its Mixtures with 10 and 30 mol % di-C2-DTP on Flotation Mass and_** 

###### **_water recovery_** 

The water recoveries in descending order were: 70% PAX//30% di-C2-DTP mixture > 90% PAX //10% di-C2-DTP mixture > pure PAX. Furthermore, there was no significant between the mass recoveries yielded by the use of pure PAX and the 70% PAX//30% di-C2-DTP mixture (Fig. 6). 



###### **Figure 6: Percentage cumulative mass vs. water recovery obtained with pure PAX collector and its mixture with di-C2-DTP at a dosage 0.488 mmol/ton and different constituents’ ratio** 

The use of the mixture 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP yielded a lower water recovery than the use of pure PAX (Fig. 6). The di-C2-DTP collector had two ethyl groups attached to it, thus its agglomerates were hydrophobic. Therefore, the presence of di-C2-DTP in the mixture resulted in the formation of more hydrophobic di-C2-DTP agglomerates. The more hydrophobic the agglomerates are, the greater their drainage and the grater the drainage the lower the water recovery. This was borne out by the higher water recovery obtained by the use of the mixture over the water recovery obtained by the use of pure PAX (Fig. 6). 

The mixture 90% PAX// 10% di-C2-DTP yielded a higher water recovery than mixture 70% PAX// 30% di-C2-DTP. The opposite results were expected as increasing di-C2-DTP concentration would increase the formation of more di-C2-DTP hydrophobic agglomerates. Thus, the mixture with higher di-C2-DTP concentration was expected to have a higher degree of drainage than the mixture with a lower concentration of di-C2-DTP. 

247 

###### **CONCLUSIONS** 

The final concentrate grades do not only depend on the selectivity of the collector, they also depend on the collector’s ability to lower water recoveries. For instance all the collectors which had higher selectivity but were unable to lower the water recovery consequently yielded lower nickel grades than the ones with lower water recovery and intermediate selectivity. The high water recoveries nullified the positive effect of selectivity as the degree of entrainment is proportional to water recovery. According to the results foun

d in this work di-C1-DTC was the better co-collector than diC2-DTP. There was no benefit in using a greater percentage of di-C1-DTC as increasing di-C1-DTC percentage from 10% to 30% increased the froth mineralisation and possibly degree of entrainement. The mixture PAX//di-C1-DTC performed better at 90:10 ratios. This ratio achieved 3.51% average nickel concentrate grade and 67.40% cumulative nickel recovery. The concentration of di-C2-DTP in the mixture 90% PAX//10% di-C2-DTP was too low to effectively affect the nickel grade and recovery. Furthermore, increasing the concentration of di-C2-DTP improved the selectivity and nickel grade. These improvements however were more evident in the first three concentrates.

Post mining the ore from the pits is delivered to the ROM pad where blending takes place to ensure equalized feed to the plant. Feed conveyors to the primary crusher are fitted with iron removal magnets to remove any carried over magnetic material coming from the mining operation. Ore from the ROM pad is sent to a single stage crushing circuit to generate a crushed product that passes 160mm. The crushing plant is designed to have 85% operating utilization out of an eight hour shift basis. The remaining time each day will be available for maintenance, offering up to 16 hours per day for scheduled maintenance purposes. This optimum power consumption was achieved utilizing an open circuit SAG mill followed by a closed circuit ball mill to grind ore down to 75% passing 75µm. The stockpiled ore from the crushing plant is reclaimed using apron feeders and fed to the milling plant at a steady rate of 135tph with 91% operating utilization. (This 91% operation utilization includes an 8 hours per week for scheduled maintenance purposes). Post the ball mill operation a cyclone is used to recover any oversized material and ensure regrinding occurs by recirculating the oversized material back to the ball mill feed end. The milled ore feeds the thickener where excess water is removed before thickener underflow is fed to two (2) separate belt filters. The dewatering steps are used to reduce the water consumption in the plant and also to prepare the leach feed with raffinate used in the leach circuit. The leach circuit consists of seven leach tanks per stage for a total residence time of 12 hours. Most of the c

opper is leached during the time in the first two tanks where Sulphuric Acid (H2SO4) is added, while the cobalt is leached in the latter tanks. Sulphur Dioxide (SO2) is added to the last three tanks to help the cobalt leach process. 

The leach product flows to the first of six (21m) counter current decantation (CCD) thickeners. 

Raffinate from the Cobalt Solvent Extraction area is added to the last CCD thickener as washing liquor. The overall wash ratio in the CCD area is approximately 1.3. 

The pinned bed clarifier overflow is pumped to the primary copper SX where copper is extracted from the PLS and loaded onto an organic LIX984N before being stripped of the organic by a 200g/l H2SO4 strip solution. The stripped organic is re-used whilst the loaded aqueous stream or advance electrolyte is pumped to the copper electrowinning plant. The cobalt rich, copper stripped, raffinate is pumped to the raffinate storage tank from where it is pumped to the filtration and leach areas as make-up solution whilst a bleed stream is sent to the cobalt recovery section of the plant. 

In the cobalt recovery section it is imperative that the electrolyte sent to cobalt electrowinning is cleaned of all metals that could co-deposit and reduce the grade of cobalt metal. The first metal removed is iron, which is oxidized to the ferric form and precipitated out using lime. 

The clarified Iron removal thickener overflow PLS flows to the secondary copper SX where the PLS is scavenged to remove any remaining copper using the stripped organic from the primary copper SX area. The clarified PLS is sent to the aluminum removal section whilst the copper loaded organic is returned to the primary copper SX area. 

The secondary copper SX PLS is further purified by precipitating out aluminum using lime. The first stage thickener underflow is pumped to the tailings treatment tank whilst the overflow flows to second stage where some more lime is added to purify the PLS further. The second stage product is sent to the second stage thickener from where the purified PLS overflow flows to the copper removal circuit where the last residual copper is removed. The underflow from the second stage thickener is returned to the iron precipitation section. 

266 

After copper precipitation the purified solution is pumped to the manganese and zinc (Mn/Zn) SX plant. In the Mn/Zn SX plant the manganese and zinc is extracted from the PLS using di-2-ethyl hexylphosphoric acid (DEHPA). The manganese and zinc is then stripped from the DEPHA using a 150g/l H2SO4 strip solution. The manganese and zinc rich aqueous phase is then pumped to tailings and effluent treatment.  The clarified PLS is pumped Cobalt SX plant. 

In the cobalt SX plant cobalt is extracted in five extraction stages using Cyanex 272 as the organic phase. The raffinate from the cobalt SX extraction phase is returned to the CCD area. The loaded organic is pumped to the cobalt SX scrubbing and stripping where the cobalt is stripped f

rom the organic. The stripped organic is returned to the extraction phase whilst the cobalt rich advance solution is pumped to the cobalt electrowinning section. 

In both the copper and cobalt electrowinning areas the advance liquor is heated through heat exchangers. Guar is added as a smoothing agent to the copper electrolyte stream. 

Copper electrolyte is pumped to the copper tank house which consists of 112 cells. Copper is plated on the cathode and the cathodes are periodically removed for stripping before the cathodes are baled for transport. Cobalt electrolyte is pumped to 52. Cobalt is plated on the cathodes and the cathodes are periodically removed for stripping. The cobalt metal plate is brittle and will be shipped in drums. 

All the discard streams in the plant are pumped to the tailings and effluent treatment tank where lime is added to neutralize the slurry before it is pumped to the tailings dam some 3.5 km from the metallurgical site. Return water from the tailings dam is pumped back to the plant and is used as part of the plant water requirements. In order to best utilize the limited water available in the area, water is re-circulated and retained in process where possible. The only water leaving the process will be in the tailings stream. 

To ensure the quality of the copper cathode and cobalt final product the final product bin and storage area will be housed in a roofed area. In addition the design provides for all the required offices, warehouses, service buildings etc. 

The process plant design criteria, inclusive of all reagent and consumable consumptions, have been developed from the results of the suite of metallurgical tests described in the Metallurgy section of this report.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The Copperbelt in Central Africa, which includes Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), are well-known mineral-rich mining areas. Interest in the Copperbelt has resurged in recent years, primarily due to the upturn in international commodity prices and

major projects have been commissioned or expanded in the Copperbelt over the past 5 years. Generally, projects in these areas produce copper metal as primary product, with an intermediate cobalt precipitate or cobalt metal as a by-product. 

Hydrometallurgical processing forms an integral part of the recovery and purification of copper and cobalt. The conventional hydrometallurgical approach for treating ores in this region involves a sulphuric acid leach circuit in a loop with Cu solvent extraction and Cu electrowinning. In order to recover and purify cobalt, a copper raffinate bleed stream is typically taken from which impurities are removed and the cobalt is upgraded in multiple unit operations. The complexity of the downstream purification of cobalt is dependent on the type and purity of cobalt product that is to be produced, and the value that could be realised for the specific product. 

Macro-economic factors such as the social and political environment, resource size, value metal grades, local infrastructure, environmental aspects, and certain other risks are critical considerations for process selection and financial investment. Some of these aspects are discussed hand-in-hand with the metallurgical processing options for projects in the Copperbelt.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

Africa has the potential to contribute significantly to meeting global requirements for refined copper and cobalt in the medium- to long-term due to the presence of the Central African Copperbelt, which contains approximately 40% and 10% of the world’s cobalt and copper reserves, respectively. The Copperbelt occupies a major geological structure called the Lufilian Arc that extends over a distance of more than 500 kilometres from Kolwezi in the southern parts of the Katanga Province, DRC, to Luanshya in neighbouring Zambia. This arc is host to extensive high-grade copper-cobalt mineralisation in very large stratiform deposits. Given the high-grade copper and cobalt mineralisation of the Copperbelt, the region will contribute significantly to meeting future global requirements for both metals in the medium- to long term<sup>(1)</sup> . 

The uniqueness of these deposits in terms of their grade, presence of valuable by-products and large tonnages amenable to low-cost bulk mining, has contributed to the Copperbelt emerging as a global ‘hotspot’ for copper investment and exploitation in recent years<sup>(1)</sup> . Even with sustained production over almost 100 years, there will remain huge resources of copper and cobalt in this extensive mineral province<sup>(15)</sup> . 

Renewed investor interest in the past ten years or so, together with surging stock and commodity markets, supported by significantly calmer internal politics has allowed for a regeneration of the mineral economies of these two countries. The upturn in international commodity prices from the end of 2003 until the middle of 2008, supported by legislative and political changes in the DRC (a new m

ining code in 2003 and the first democratic elections in 2006) and a favourable (at the time) tax and royalty regime in Zambia, sparked a revival of interest in both re-establishing existing operations and exploring for and developing new mines in both countries. Although the industry experienced a significant setback following the drop in copper prices in the wake of the global recession, the sector is currently experiencing a turnaround and the future outlook looks favourable. Unlike the political turmoil of earlier decades, the crisis appears to have left the Copperbelt mining sector a lot more resilient than before. In the DRC, operations are comparably more recent and the pipeline involves exploration, development and operating plants. 

The production of copper plays a key role in Zambia’s economic activities and since 2003, been a key force behind the country’s annual economic growth rate of 5%. Zambia is currently ranked has as the seventh largest producer of copper in the world with an excess of 2Bt of copper still to be extracted. Since 1995, the DRC government has been engaged in a process of privatisation of its mining assets which contain estimated reserves of 30 Mt of copper and 3 Mt of cobalt. The giant mining parastatal, Gйcamines, has entered into various joint venture agreements with foreign mining firms in an attempt to improve its declining production rates and rekindle mining activities along the Copperbelt. 

Copper production in the DRC and Zambia has been increasing year-on-year since the late-1990s. Collectively these two countries account for 2.1% and 4% of world copper production respectively, and this is expected to rise to 4.9% and 5.7% by 2013. Copper output in the region could rise from around 1.2 Mt to nearly 3 Mt by 2015, positioning the Copperbelt as the second largest producing region after Chile. The DRC and Zambia account for 40% and 20%, respectively, of current (88kt in 2010) global cobalt production. Around 40 to 50% of incremental global production of the next five years is projected to arise from the DRC<sup>(2)</sup> . Furthermore the long history of mining in the Copperbelt with inefficient extraction technology in the past has resulted in plant tailings as another important source for copper and cobalt. Retreatment of such wastes is seen as a high potential source of copper and cobalt and therefore investment in such actives is increasing in conjunction with other projects. Aside from exploration potential, there is also a high level of interest from Asian investors for off-take potential. Further, large deposits that have not yet been explored using modern technology create an opportunity for expanding and developing new operations over the longerterm<sup>(16)</sup>
