###### **MORTARS FOR ACID RESISTANT BRICK LININGS IN HYDROMETALLURICAL APPLICATIONS** 

By 

###### **Kevin Brooks** 

Koch Knight LLC, USA 

Presented by 

###### **Mark W Martin** 

Koch Australia, Koch Knight Division mark.martin@kochknight.com 

Corresponding Author 

###### **Kevin Brooks** 

Koch Knight LLC, USA 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The application of hydrometallurgy in the recovery of nickel, copper gold and other metals continues to grow. Acid brick linings have been proven to provide economical and reliable service in acid leach vessels, pressure oxidation autoclaves, pressure let down vessels, and other related equipment. Careful attention must be given to all of the components including the mortar selection and application to achieve a reliable lining system. An understanding of the properties and limitations of the mortar as well as the process conditions will allow for the selection of the best mortars to provide a reliable lining. 

313 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

###### **Application** 

The application of hydrometallurgy in the recovery of nickel, copper gold and other metals continues to grow. The acidic nature and higher temperatures of some of these processes limit the use of alloys, fiberglass or other materials of construction for the vessels. Acid brick linings have been proven to provide economical and reliable service in acid leach vessels, pressure oxidation autoclaves, pressure let down vessels, and other related equipment. In addition to hydrometallurgy, acid brick lining systems also have a long history of operation in the chemical industry under similar operating conditions. 

Acid brick linings are composite systems with several key components including a corrosion resistant membrane applied the vessel shell, protected by the acid brick working face that is laid up in the corrosion resistant mortar used to bond the brick together. Careful attention must be given to all of the component parts of these systems, including the mortar selection and

application techniques, if the designer hopes to deliver a reliable lining system. A variety of mortars are used in these applications that are specifically formulated to withstand the process conditions. Consideration must be given to the process chemistry, operating temperatures and mechanical requirements when selecting which mortar to use. 

###### **MORTAR TYPES** 

###### **Mortar Types** 

Acid resistant mortars fall into two broad categories. The first category is silicate based mortars. These are based upon various silicate solutions with inert aggregates. The second category is mortars based upon on thermoset resins which include a catalyzed resin and select aggregates. For both categories the aggregates are typically fine size graded silica powders. Carbon powder, silicon carbide and mineral oxides can also be incorporated into the aggregates for some mortar mixes. Another type of mortar used in pressure oxidation service, which falls outside of these categories, is litharge mortar. 

###### **Silicate Mortars** 

Silicate mortars are generally two component systems consisting of a silicate solution and silica based aggregate. Formulas based on potassium, sodium and colloidal silicate solutions are available. It is important to select the silicate mortar that is formulated for the intended application. Some silicate mortars are made specifically for concentrated sulfuric acid for use in sulfuric acid absorption and drying towers. Other formulas are adjusted to allow for improved resistance at lower concentrations and exposure to saturated steam and condensates. 

In hydrometallurgical applications potassium silicate based mortars are used most often in equipment such as pressure oxidation autoclaves and other vessels that operate at higher temperatures. As silicate based mortars are inorganic, they are not oxidized at higher temperatures or in oxygen enriched environments. Silicate mortars can be susceptible to wash out in both acidic and saturated steam environments 

. 

###### **Thermoset Resin Based Mortars** 

Thermoset mortars are based upon the same type of polymer resins used in the fabrication of fiberglass equipment. The resin systems used include vinyl esters, furfuryl alcohols, phenolics, epoxies and other similar resins. These mortars can be either two or three components. Some manufacturers incorporate the catalyst into the aggregate while others provide the catalyst separately so that its addition can be varied to adjust set times 

. 

When they are suitable for the process conditions, thermoset mortars are preferred due to their stronger bond strengths and lower porosity. The use of thermoset mortars are limited by operating temperature. Most mortars in this category have maximum allowable service temperatures of 150-200 °C.  Thermoset mortars also are not suitable for oxygen rich conditions such as in pressure oxidation autoclaves and the concentrated sulfuric acids found in sulfuric acid plants. 

314 

The most comm

on thermoset mortars used in hydrometallurgical applications are silica filled vinyl esters and furfuryl alcohols. They generally are used to install the brick linings in pressure let down (flash) vessels, back courses of pressure leach vessels, ambient leach vessels, blast spools and other vessels with similar operating conditions. 

###### **Litharge Mortars** 

Litharge mortars are formed from the mixing of glycerol with lead oxide to form a metallic glyceride. Litharge mortars are used primarily in the vapor zones of autoclaves where they have demonstrated good resistance to wash out in the steam environment. They also exhibit a unique property of having a lower modulus of elasticity at operating temperatures. This allows the mortar to relieve high stress points when the lining is in service. Litharge mortars do require extensive specific health and safety precautions that include items such as negative air containment, HEPA filter respirators and hazardous waste disposal. 

###### **CURING** 

###### **Cure Mechanism** 

The curing mechanisms for silicate and thermoset mortars are different. Silicate mortars require the silicate solution to gel through the use of setting agents that are incorporated in the aggregate and react with the silicate solution when the two components are mixed. Thermoset mortars are based upon polymerization of the resin. Catalysts used to drive the polymerization reactions are either premixed in the aggregate or added separately as a third component to thermoset mortars. 

###### **Acid Cure** 

Earlier formulations of silicate mortars required the application of an acid wash to promote curing. In some instances this practice is continuing today even though research has shown that the acid wash has limited value. See the ALTA 2005 paper “Acid Brick Expansion Explained” for more detail on the mechanics of acid curing vessel linings without acid washing. Silicate mortars of today use improved setting agents mixed into the aggregate at the factory, so liquid acid sprays on the “green” joint surface has limited value as a method of curing the mortars. Careful mortar mixing at the factory and the jobsite, combined with high quality setting agents in the powder, will give good finished mortar joints without an acid wash. Unless specified by the manufacturer, an “acid cure” or “acid wash” is not required for silicate mortars. 

Thermoset mortars cure as the polymers and catalysts react. Any attempt to wet acid cure these mortars is likely to interfere with the crosslinking reactions. When installing thermoset mortars, managing ambient temperature in the vessel and keeping the work area dry are the important factors to control in order to fully cure the mortar. 

###### **Cure Time** 

In all cases, mortars should be allowed to air cure fully before being placed in service. The cure time for acid resistant mortars will vary with the type of mortar, temperature and humidity. Most acid resistant mortars have a working life o

f 30-45 minutes and take an initial set in 24-48 hours. The polymer based reactions of thermoset mortars occur faster than those of silicate mortars. Although silicate mortars achieve an initial set quickly, the ultimate strength for silicate mortars is not reached for several days. 

The quickest cure times are achieved with lower humidity and higher ambient temperatures. Low humidity allows silicate mortars and furfuryl mortars to expel excess water that is generated as part of the gelling or polymer reaction. Most mortars require a minimum curing temperature of 10 °C with optimum curing rates at temperatures of 20-30 °C. Curing times are accelerated at higher temperatures. 

315 

###### **MIXING** 

In order to achieve optimal performance, care must be taken when mixing acid resistant mortars. Multi-component mortars are designed for combination in specific mix ratios by weight. Typical mix ratios are one part solution or resin with two to three parts aggregate. Deviation from the mix ratio can result in the addition of too much or too little catalyst resulting in mortars that either cure exceedingly quickly or don’t cure at all. Adequate mix time must also be allowed for in order to ensure that the components are thoroughly mixed together and the catalyst or setting agent is completely incorporated into the mix. 

The mortar mixing equipment must be compatible with the mortar type. Air entrainment should be avoided in order to minimize the porosity of the mortar.  Finer aggregates can become airborne and not be incorporated into the mortar if the mixer speeds are too high. 

When mixing must take place at less than desirable ambient conditions, it may be useful to warm or cool the mortar components prior to mixing. For lower installation temperatures the mortar components (and the bricks being installed) can be warmed to 20-30 °C to reduce the set time. Thermoset mortars that are used at higher installation temperatures can be cooled before mixing to extend their working life, and installed from ice cooled mortar pans at the bricklayers’ working stations. 

###### **TESTING** 

Mortar testing can be challenging as it is difficult to simulate the mechanical properties of mortars installed as thin (3 to 5 mm thick) mortar joints. For convenience it is more common to test small cylinders of mortar. Test cylinders provide data useful for quality assurance purposes, comparison of mortars and to measure improvements. Care should be taken when extrapolating these results as input values for mechanical design. 

Recently, test cylinders made on a job at 50 mm diameter indicated mortar strengths well below normal. Checking the QC data from the factory did not show any indication of low strength as manufactured. The mixing and handling of the mortar at the jobsite was done to acceptable standards. Further testing of 25 mm cylinders side by side with 50 mm cylinders revealed that the cylinder size was the reason for the erroneous data: The larger diame

ter samples were not curing completely. Reviewing the sampling protocols with the mortar manufacturer is highly recommended to assure accurate test results. 

Test methods are available in the both the ASTM and DIN-EN standards for testing acid resistant mortars.  In addition to their chemical resistance, typical physical properties that are considered for acid resistant mortars are bond strength, absorption, compressive strength and tensile strength. Bond strength is a measure of the bond between the mortar and brick. This can vary with the surface finish and porosity of the brick. 

For many established process chemistries, the mortar selection has been established by previous practice. When selecting mortars for new process conditions, testing should be performed by exposing the potential mortar candidates to conditions that most closely match those anticipated in the production equipment. The ideal environment for exposure testing of new processes is in the pilot plant. Useful data for analyzing the performance of the mortar after exposure is weight loss, change in compressive strength and change in chemistry. The best mortars will show little change after exposure when compared to control samples. 

Absorption is measured as a percentage of the total volume that can be saturated with a liquid. All acid resistant mortars and brick have some degree of porosity. Mortars with lower absorptions are desirable in order to limit any acidic leaching to the surface of the lining. 

Most vessel linings are cylindrical configurations, allowing for linings that are maintained under compression once they are keyed in. Generally mortars have lower compressive strengths than bricks and are the limiting factor for linings with high compressive loads. When installed as a mortar joint the mortar is subjected to biaxial and triaxial loads. Under these conditions the mortar can withstand compressive forces as much as two to six times greater than those measured with standardized uniaxial test methods. This property increases the allowable stress limits for the mortar. 

316 

Tensile strengths of acid resistant mortars tend to be of a similar order of magnitude as the standard silica-alumina acid resistant bricks usually being installed. Typical values are on the order of 2-6 MPa. Tensile strength values only become a consideration if there are unusual geometries that result in tensile stresses at the working face of the lining. 

###### **HYDROMETALlURGICAL APPLICATIONS** 

###### **Pressure Oxidation Autoclaves** 

One of the most challenging applications for acid resistant mortars is in pressure oxidation autoclaves. The operating temperature is often above the allowable limit for thermoset mortars and the oxygen over pressure also precludes the use of resin based mortars. The saturated steam and steam condensate in the vapor zone causes softening and washout of standard silicate mortars. Current practice is to use multiple types of mortar in the lining desig

n to address the requirements in specific sections of the autoclave lining. The primary components of the autoclave lining includes the slurry zone which is full immersed during operation, vapor zone above the slurry level and the interface between the two.  Modified mortar grouts are also used to grout the nozzle inserts. 

Halogen free potassium silicate mortars with inorganic hardeners are used to line the slurry zone. Potassium silicate mortars that are formulated for weak sulfuric acid strengths (2-10%) provide good performance in this area. 

The vapor zone and interface zones are more challenging, and can exhibit different degrees of mortar washout depending on the operation. This is addressed with either litharge mortars or silicate based mortars that have been developed specifically for this application. Care must be taken when selecting vapor zone mortars because the vapor zones have a large concentration of nozzle openings to accommodate the various process needs. These clusters of nozzles create higher concentrated stresses in the lining at these points. Mortars that are selected solely for chemical resistance may make for a brick lining system that is too brittle and result in spalling of the acid resistant brick. Modeling these areas with analytical methods such as finite element analysis (FEA) are being applied to confirm the stresses in these areas. Mortar selections can then be adjusted to best meet the conditions at these mechanically complex points in the lining. 

###### **Flash Vessels** 

Another application for acid resistant mortars in pressure oxidation plants is the lining of flash vessels. Most flash vessels operate within the range were thermoset mortars can be used. Either vinyl ester or furfuryl resin based mortars are used depending on the lining supplier’s preference. These mortars have both been proven to be reliable in this service. 

In nickel laterite acid leaching, the high pressure flash vessels operate at temperatures similar to pressure oxidation autoclaves. Silicate mortars are used in this case and brick product selection is also similar to autoclave applications. The medium and low pressure flash vessels can be lined using thermoset mortars. 

###### **Ambient Leach Vessels** 

Ambient leach vessels that are lined with acid brick operate at temperature just above where rubber only linings do not provide reliable service. This is in the range of 100-120 °C. Vinyl ester or furfuryl resin based mortars are also used for this application. Some of the leach vessels in this service are very large in diameter and use thin brick linings, minimizing the keying effect of the brick lining. In these cases it becomes more important to consider the bond strength of the mortar. 

###### **CONCLUSION** 

Acid resistant mortars are an important consideration when selecting and designing acid resistant lining systems. Hydrometallurgical applications have unique demands that the mortars must meet for long lining life. Sele

ction of reliable mortars requires understanding the properties and limitations of the various mortars available as well as the process conditions. When the acid resistant mortar is incorporated into a well designed and carefully installed lining system, reliable vessel linings can be achieved for hydrometallurgical applications.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Many low grade nickel sulphide ores are hosted in gangue containing high levels of magnesium silicates, which consequently consume a large amount of sulphuric acid in conventional bacterial leaching scenarios where solution pH’s below 2 are required. BioHeap has developed a saline tolerant bacterial culture using patented methods, that is capable of operating at elevated pH’s at levels where ferric iron precipitates out of solution. Operating at elevated pH has the dual advantage of significantly reducing the acid consumption and reducing limestone demand for iron disposal. 

Further work is planned to critically compare the performance of the high pH culture against cultures operating at conventional pH and to expand the range of cultures that are capable of operating at high pH. 

380

###### **Introduction of Western Areas and BioHeap**

###### **EXISTING LEACHING CONDITIONS** 

Bioleaching is a process whereby microorganisms catalyze the dissolution of valuable metals from ores into solution. In general, the dissolution of mineral sulfides in bacterial systems, is the results of ferric iron and proton attack via the polysulfide pathway (Rohwerder et al., 2008). The conditions for such a reaction to occur are generally dictated by the ability of the microorganism to catalyze the leaching process efficiently. 

Previous studies have demonstrated that bioleaching of mineral sulfides occurs favorably at pH <3 (Halinen et al., 2009), with majority of heap bioleaching processes of low grade ore are treated with a solution pH between 1.5 to 2.5 (Plumb et al., 2008). At such pH conditions, the bio-oxidation acidophilic microorganisms convert ferrous ion to ferric ion which is needed for the leaching of sulfide minerals. 

Bioleaching of materials at a high pH range has been studied in the past (Cameron,

et al., 2009a; Cameron, et al., 2009b; Cameron, et al., 2010; Halinen et al., 2009; Plumb et al., 2008) .The majority of results published suggested that beyond a pH of 2 the rate of leaching is significantly decreased and the percentage of metals recovery is reduced (Plumb et al., 2008). Halinen et al., 2009 reported the rate of bioleaching of nickel and zinc at pH 1.5 is 3-4 times faster than the rate of 

381 

leaching observed at pH 3.  It is suggested that the lack of dissolved ferric ion and diffusion barriers created by iron oxide precipitates minimized the rate of leaching at pH 2.5 to 3. 

Interestingly, Cameron et al. (2009a; 2009b; 2010) , has successfully demonstrated bioleaching of low-grade ultramafic nickel suphide ore at temperature 30 °C and 45 °C at pH 3 by mixed microbial culture previously adapted to the ore. The success of Cameron’s studies may be largely contributed to the adaptating of the microbes to specific conditions and feed materials prior to the bioleaching procedure. The use of adapted microorganisms prior to leaching can enhance the leaching efficiency by 2 to 4 times when compared to unadapted culture (Li and Ke, 2001a; Li and Ke, 2001b). 

###### **WHY DO WE WANT TO LEACH AT HIGHER PH?** 

Bioleaching of metal sulphides at extreme pH (<2) can result in the dissolution of gangue materials. Undesirably cations, such as aluminium, manganese, amorphous silica and specifically, excessive ferric, can further result in releasing toxic trace elements, thickening of leach liquor thus potentially interfering with liquid flow in heap leaching, formation of passivation of sulphide minerals by jarosite formation or can be problematic during recovery of base metals during refining (Dopso et al., 2009, Halinen et al., 2009). Final effluents from bioleaching operation generally have to be neutralized and to remove iron and sulphate as stable end products by the addition of limestone or lime to increase of the pH of effluent to approximately 3. Therefore, bioleaching of metals at high pH may potentially improve the downstream metals recovery processes, as well as reducing the operating costs. 

The mineralogy of the specific ore can have a significant impact on the acid consumption properties and solution composition of the bacterial leaching system. Depending on the composition of the feed sample, the dissolution of mineral sulfides can be classified as either acid-producing or acid consuming. The majority of the gangue present in most ore samples, include magnesium silicates, and are acid consuming (Rawlings et al., 2003; Strцmberg and Banwart, 1999). Therefore, maintaining of solution pH within a desirable range with the addition of sulfuric acid can be a major cost during a bioleaching operation (Watling, 2006). The application of pre-leaching of ore containing high levels of magnesium gangue prior to the bioleaching phase has been shown to reduce time required to stabilize the pH level between 1.7 – 2.2 (Zhen et al., 2009;

Qin et al., 2009) . However, such a method has resulted in higher overall acid consumption at greater than 600 g kg<sup>-1</sup> ore (Zhen et al., 2009; Qin et al., 2009). Halinen et. al. (2009) has demonstrated that an increase of pH from 1.5 to 2.0 during the column leaching of a particular black schist ore can reduce the acid consumption from 160 g kg<sup>-1</sup> ore to 38 g kg<sup>-1</sup> ore. 

###### **BIOHEAP DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM** 

###### **Methodology** 

###### **_Bacterial_** 

For development of cultures capable of operating at high pH’s, it was advantageous to select a starting culture that was not dependent on high ferric levels for leaching to progress. Both BioHeap’s chalcopyrite and saline tolerant cultures naturally operate in low ferric environments at conventional pH’s (below 2), and the saline culture was chosen as the starting point, as it also operates in low total iron environments due to tendency of the iron to precipitate in the highly saline environment. As ferric iron begins to precipitate beyond pH 3 due to exceeding the solubility product, in a similar manner that precipitation is noted in BioHeap’s saline culture, this culture was thought to be the best match to the proposed leaching conditions. Using BioHeap’s patented procedures, this culture was then adapted to operate at higher pH’s. 

BioHeap culture, Ni-S-J065B, was used in these studies. The cultures were grown in 3L stirred tank reactors and were maintained on nickel concentrate suspended in water. The desirable pH of the solution was achieved by addition of concentrated sulphuric acid. A customised water bath was used to regulate the temperature in the bioreactor at approximately 55 °C and aeration was provided to the culture by compressed air introduced into the mixing zone of the reactor 

Prior to it use, Ni-S-J065B was adapted to saline condition of 100g/L Cl- (115 g/L TDS). , and a sub-culture of Ni-S-J065B was gradually adapted to a solution pH of 3.5. To distinguish the newly developed culture from the original inoculum, it was renamed to Ni-S-J069B.

###### **_Sample Preparation of High Magnesia Ore_** 

A high magnesia ore sample, J062A, was split using rotary splitter to provide samples as feed for bacterial development work and metallurgical analysis. A Head sample of the ore was assayed for 2- 2- Ni, Co, Zn, Cu,  Fe, Al, Ca, Mg, Mn, S (Total), S (Elemental), S2- (Sulphide), SO4 , C (Total), CO3 , and an ICP Scan. 

Acid consumption studies were carried out on sample crushed to P100= 9.5mm using a bottle roll technique. Concentrated sulphuric acid was used to maintain the solution at pH 1.8 to simulate conventional bioleaching conditions. Acid addition was recorded and used to calculate the total quantity of acid consumed by the ore.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The need for copper and molybdenum continues to grow as does the need for clean efficient metallurgical technologies capable of treating mixed metal concentrates. Currently, the use of hydrometallurgical pressure oxidation for copper concentrate treatment is growing. Furthermore, with limited molybdenum roasting capacity, stringent industrial molybdenum concentrate roaster feed specifications, poor rhenium recoveries, and the inherent environmental issues associated with pyrometallurgical treatments, hydrometallurgical options are also now being pursued for molybdenum concentrates. Moreover, given the inherent grade, recovery and cost inefficiencies in the differential flotation process normally employed for molybdenum concentrates produced as a by-product of copper mining, there is a growing need to directly treat combined bulk copper and molybdenum concentrates. This minimizes molybdenum concentrate roasting limitations, specifications and requirements, while allowing simplification of increased efficiency of and cost reductions in upstream mineral processing circuits now producing separate copper and molybdenum concentrates by differential flotation. It would also allow more direct and efficient recovery of rhenium. Finally, hydrometallurgical technology will also reduce the need for costly final molybdenum concentrate impurity treatment circuits, thereby allowing for lower grade mixed metal molybdenum concentrates to be treated directly for a greater metal value realization. In summary, industrial nitrogen species catalyzed (i.e. NSC) hydrometallurgical pressure oxidation has many advantages over conventional pressure oxidation systems and offers a tangible process route to treat mixed bulk concentrates. This updated study illustrates the fundamental concepts, confirmatory testing, application, proposed design and associated cost estimates for the development and industrial implementation of this proven mode of hydrometallurgical processing as applied to copper, molybdenum, rhenium concentrates.

This inherent asset of the unique system eliminates the need for the use of high temperatures and high pressures, which lead to higher costs in other pressure leach processes. For example, commonly available stainless steel can be used for the reactor vessel. And, complete oxidation of sulfide to sulfate can be achieved without the excessive conditions found in other pressure leach systems. Thus, the rapid kinetics of the system leads to smaller reactor volumes and higher unit throughputs. Finally, 99.9% of the nitrogen species utilized in the leach system report to the gas phase when the pressure vessel is flashed and they are readily destroyed and cont

ained by commercially available scrubber systems. So, environmental impacts are minimized and the NSC leach plant solutions contain little or no nitrogen species. 

###### **COPPER AND MOLYBDENUM FLOTATION CONSIDERATIONS** 

Traditional treatment of copper porphyry ores bearing molybdenum consists of differential flotation to produce two concentrates. As illustrated in Figure 1<sup>(6)</sup> , after comminution, a bulk copper and molybdenum concentrate is produced and then cleaned to increase grade but diminish recovery. Then, the copper is depressed from the bulk concentrate to produce a molybdenum concentrate and a copper concentrate. In order to meet grade constraints in the molybdenum concentrate, several stages of cleaner flotation followed by chemical leaching is required to minimize impurities. As such, as illustrated in Table 2<sup>(7)</sup> , based on worldwide operating data, less than 50% of the molybdenum is finally recovered to the concentrate. This after full costs have been absorbed for mining and milling. Then typically, the molybdenum and copper concentrates are shipped for smelting. In the case of molybdenum, since global roasting capacity is limited, concentrate impurity penalties are stringent and smelting terms can be expensive. Further, little if any credit for by product rhenium is realized. As seen in Table 3<sup>(8)</sup> , in general, there is a significant economic driver in flotation plants for lowering both capital and operating costs by making a single concentrate. At a processing rate of 20,000 tonnes per day of ore, both the CAPEX and OPEX are reduced about 8%. The actual savings is about $12 million dollars in capital and annual savings in operating cost of about $4 million dollars. Based solely on this cost saving consideration over ten years of processing, the next positive effect on NPV at a 5% discount rate before taxes is about $40 million dollars. At a processing rate of 40,000 tonnes per day, both the CAPEX drops about 6% while OPEX drops 8%. The actual savings is about $18 million dollars in capital expense and annual savings in operating cost of about $7 million dollars. Based solely on this cost saving consideration over ten years of processing, the next positive effect on NPV at a 5% discount rate before taxes is about $70 million dollars. Further, without the differential flotation or rigorous cleaning stages required, copper and, more importantly, molybdenum recoveries will increase. Given the hydrophobic nature of molybdenum, it is reasonable to assume that recoveries over 90 % would be readily achieved to a bulk concentrate. Lastly, as will be elucidated further on in the paper, on site hydrometallurgical treatment of the bulk concentrates can provide high quality copper cathode, high purity molybdenum trioxide and the potential for by product rhenium recovery credits that may not occur with traditional off site smelting.

###### **DEVELOPMENTS IN THE TREATMENT OF COPPER-ARSENIC CONCENTRATES** 

By 

1Ken Baxter, 1Iman Ghanad, 2David Dixon 

1SNC-Lavalin, Australia 

2The University of British Columbia, Canada 

Presenter and Corresponding Author 

**Ken Baxter** Ken.Baxter@snclavalin.com 

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Treatment of copper-arsenic concentrates has in the past presented technical difficulties both in achieving acceptable copper leach recoveries and fixing the arsenic in an environmentally acceptable form. Arsenic grades in copper concentrate in excess of 0.5% As are difficult to ship globally and to place with smelters. A hydrometallurgical alternative to smelting is presented which provi

des high copper recoveries and stabilises the arsenic as scorodite in the residues. 

Ongoing testwork on the Galvanox™ process at the University of British Columbia (UBC) has identified an alternative catalyst suited to leaching copper-arsenic minerals and subsequent piloting has confirmed its utility. 

A modified Galvanox™ flowsheet comprising an atmospheric leach circuit followed by solid/liquid separation and copper SX/EW has been developed based on this work where activated carbon is used to catalyse copper-arsenic minerals and pyrite oxidation is used to heat the reactors and provide iron to precipitate the arsenic leached as scorodite. The autoclave required in the typical Galvanox™ circuit is not required for this circuit configuration. 

Capital and operating costs for this flowsheet have been developed. 

416 

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

The presence of arsenic in copper ores is a common deterrent to the development of such deposits. There are many such deposits, particularly in the Americas that are in this category and this paper details a flow sheet that should find common application to treating concentrates derived from these deposits. 

Typically copper deposits are treated by flotation followed by toll treatment at a smelter, and, while the gold industry has largely adopted treatment routes that deal with high-arsenic concentrates, ores in which copper is the predominant element of value have been typically avoided when they contain high concentrations of arsenic. In addition, the environmental regulations relating to treatment of arsenic-containing materials and arsenic disposal have gradually become more stringent, creating additional challenges for the exploitation of such deposits. 

Typically mining companies are interested in minimizing capital expenditure to produce a saleable copper concentrate using conventional and well known technology to minimise project risk. However, capital expenditures on these projects are substantial, so risking the project revenue stream on hydrometallurgical treatment of concentrates is not favoured. 

When considering the exploitation of an arsenic-containing copper deposit, the following approaches may typically be explored: 

- a) Avoid the arsenic-bearing zones in the ore body. 

- b) Exclude the arsenic bearing minerals from copper concentrate during processing. 

- c) Treat arsenic-containing concentrates in a dedicated facility to produce copper and arsenic as separate products 

The approach ultimately adopted depends on a multitude of factors specific to each project, which include the abundance, occurrence and distribution of arsenic minerals, relative contribution from gold, ore behaviour during testing, etc. 

Where avoidance of arsenic-rich areas is not practical, 

- (a) Consideration may be given to physical separation of arsenic containing minerals such as tennantite and enargite from chalcopyrite, chalcocite and pyrite by selective flotation 

- (b) SNC-Lavalin has defined a s

trategy for the treatment of such ores 

- (c) In the first instance, and for deposits where arsenic grades are low, the focus is toward producing two concentrates, a copper concentrate low in arsenic suitable for a smelter, and a concentrate high in arsenic that can be treated in a hydrometallurgical plant. Where high arsenic grades preclude a dual concentrate approach then the entire flotation concentrate will require hydrometallurgical treatment. 

The selective flotation of the arsenic-containing minerals may be achieved by manipulation of flotation pH, oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), temperature as well as optimisation of the grind. Such methods have recently been developed and described<sup>(1-3)while other methods remain</sup> proprietary and confidential. Applying such a method could potentially produce an arsenic-depleted copper concentrate which can be smelted, while the arsenic-rich concentrate may be considered for disposal or, more likely, further processing as per approach (c) above. This type of approach can be considered in the first instance to reduce to mass of arsenic-containing concentrate to be treated. Production of a low arsenic concentrate for sale also reduces the overall project risk by providing part of the revenue stream via this saleable concentrate. 

When a copper concentrate is produced that contains arsenic above the shipment/smelter threshold the arsenic can be treated hydrometallurgically to produce copper cathode and gold products for sale, while fixing the arsenic in an environmentally acceptable product for disposal. 

This paper details a flow sheet developed for the treatment of high-arsenic copper concentrates, which addresses the key practical and technical issues raised above at a realistic capital and operating cost and with minimal technical risk.

Batch leaching experiments were conducted in 3-L jacketed glass stirred-tank reactors (Applikon Biotechnology) which were sealed and equipped with two stainless

###### **Summary** 

Following the batch test work, a pilot plant program was executed to address the following: 

- Confirm batch leach test chemistry and copper recovery on a continuous basis

The atmospheric leach circuit component of the overall flow sheet was piloted in a cascade of four reactors. Over 98.5% copper extraction was achieved during the pilot plant operation. ###### **PROCESS CHEMISTRY** 

The chemistry of the leaching reactions for primary copper and copper-arsenic sulphides occurring in the atmospheric leach is discussed in this section of the paper. 

###### **_Enargite Leaching_** 

The major copper arsenic mineral in the concentrate tested is enargite, comprising 44% of the concentrate. The leach process is essentially a catalysed ferric leach and the overall reaction can be written as following: 

2 Cu3 AsS4(s) + 3 H2SO4(aq) + 10 O2(g) → 6 CuSO4(aq) + 2 H3AsO4(aq) + 5 S<sup>0</sup> (s) 

###### **_Tennantite/Luzonite_** 

Minor arsenic-bearing copper sulphides are also present in the concentrate. Overall leaching reactions are: 





###### **_Chalcopyrite Leaching_** 

Chalcopyrite is present in the concentrate as a minor component and approximately 90% of the sulphide sulphur will report to the leach residue as elemental sulphur. 

423 

CuFeS2(s) + 2 H2SO4(aq) + O2(g) → CuSO4(aq) + FeSO4(aq) + 2 H2O(aq) + 2 S<sup>0</sup> (s) 

###### **_Pyrite Leaching_** 

Pyrite leaching does not occur to any extent until the majority of the copper sulphides have been leached. Pyrite leaching follows two paths with approximately 60% of the sulphide sulphur converted to sulphate and 40% to elemental sulphur. The leaching of pyrite would appear to be assisted by arsenic in solution. 



2 FeS2(s) + 2 H2SO4(aq) + O2(g) → 2 FeSO4(aq) +

2 H2O(aq) +  4 S<sup>0</sup> 

(s) 

###### **_Ferrous/Ferric Oxidation_** 

Galvanox<sup>TM</sup> is a ferric leach process, requiring regeneration ferric to ferrous a number of times within the residence time of the reactors. 

4 FeSO4(aq) + O2(g) + 2 H2SO4(aq) → 2 Fe2(SO4)3(aq) + 2 H2O(aq) 

###### **_Oxygen Utilisation_** 

The leaching of copper sulphides is controlled by the oxygen uptake to the reactors, so there is a significant scale-up issue to be addressed in moving from lab scale testwork to full scale operation. The sparging system needs to be carefully designed to maximise oxygen utilisation. 

###### **_Arsenic Precipitation_** 

Pyrite is leached in the reactor bank, largely in the final reactor tanks, providing a source of ferric iron to precipitate the arsenic in a controlled manner as scorodite. The majority of the iron leached comes from pyrite leaching with some contribution from chalcopyrite. The discharge temperature from the atmospheric leach is typically in the range 90–95<sup>o</sup> C, which is ideal for scorodite precipitation. The majority of the leach is run at 85<sup>o</sup> C. Of the iron arsenate compounds, scorodite is one of the most stable compounds across a wide range of pH levels. It reaches its lowest solubility levels at neutral pH levels. Arsenic levels in solution following precipitation are in the 0–10 ppm range. The slow release of iron and arsenic into solution favors the formation of scorodite in preference to ferric arsenate which would require substantially higher levels of iron to generate. The optimum conditions and kinetics of precipitation have been studied at length by Demopoulos et al.<sup>(8-10)</sup> and require a combination of seeding and supersaturation control. The solution chemistry of the continuous reactor bank identifies partial precipitation of arsenic throughout the reactors, and control of reactor acidity assists in ensuring arsenic precipitation as scorodite together with gypsum precipitation. There is some evidence in the work of Demopoulos to suggest that the presence of gypsum in the arsenic-iron residues may contribute favorably to the stability of the residues and staged precipitation as can be seen in the continuous reactors also has a positive impact on arsenic stability.

Chloride process uses reaction of chlorine with titanium in the feed material to form TiCl 4 , which is later reacted with oxygen to form TiO 2 . The sulphate process uses leaching with sulfuric acid to bring titanium in solution. Hydrated titanium dioxide is precipitated from the solution and calcined to make titanium dioxide. cifications for making pigment grade TiO</mark> 2 <mark>are very strict, and require extreme control of other transition metal elements, which can make the color of pigment off-white and unacceptable. PRO proprietary process consists of leaching ilmenite ore/concentrate in a HCl-MgCl2 lixiviant thereby bringing Ti, Fe, V and other metals in solution. After solid-liquid separation, pregnant liquor is subjected to Stage 1 solvent extraction for iron removal. This results in Fe-rich preg strip, which can be subjected to pyrohydrolysis for the production of iron oxide and regeneration of acid for recycle and Fe-deficient raffinate. Hydrated TiO2 is produced by thermal precipitation from the Ti-rich strip liquor. Rutile TiO2 is produced after drying and calcinations of the precipitate. Precipitation and calcinations conditions can be controlled to produce anatase TiO2 as well. Process conditions can be controlled to produce nano-sized TiO2 with particle size of 20-40 nm as well as particles in the range of 250-300 nm for application as pigment. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

In this paper, hydrometallurgical process steps for separating metals from iron bearing brines, which could be suitable for processing complex ores, are presented. These process steps include pyrohydrolysis, vacuum evaporation, autoclave oxidation, selective ferric chloride hydrolysis, and selective metal chloride crystallization. 

For the separation of nickel and cobalt from iron, experiments concerning the hydrolysis of ferric chloride are performed. It can be shown that produced hematite contains only traces of nickel and cobalt. In another set of experiments, nickel chloride and cobalt chloride are selectively precipitated from a ferric chloride solution by increasing the free hydrogen chloride concentration in the solution. 

Based on the experiments performed, an exemplary flow sheet for processing a representative nickel laterite ore is presented. Based on the assumptions made, for an iron-to-nickel-ratio of 20:1, approx. 510 MJ of caloric energy are necessary for delivering 1 kg nickel (as nickel chloride dihydrate). 

Challenges and risks of introducing new chloride hydromet processes are discussed in this paper; reference is also made to some experience gained while building the first large scale hydrolytic distillation facility for ferrous chloride at a customer in Alabama, USA.

###### **INTRODUCTION** 

By 2050, the world’s population is expected to grow from a 2012 level of 7 billion to between 8 and 10 billion people. Most of this growth is expected to happen in Asia and Africa.

It will very likely be accompanied by a massive wave of urbanization, which, if historical examples are a valid predictor, will first trigger the need for the provision of a suitable public and industrial infrastructure and then yield a ramp-up in personal consumption. 

Energy, water and resources will be in growing demand. To limit the scope of this paper and to safely remain within SMS Siemag’s comfort zone of expertise, we shall focus on one of the major subsets of the resources category – namely, metals. 

Several metals suppliers may soon be able to match market demand only if they start tackling low-grade ore bodies, or ores of a nature that poses significant challenges to the designers of extraction processes, and that have a long history of being shunned by miners, for good reasons. The easy-to-mine ore is running out, or is found in locations where it appears rather difficult to install and maintain the required mining and/or refinery infrastructure. 

Our company is one of world’s leading suppliers in the field of chemical metal surface treatment and hydrochloric acid regeneration. SMS Siemag’s core hydromet technology is called pyrohydrolysis and we are applying it all over the world to recover HCl from spent pickle liquors in the steel industry. It may not be too much of a surprise to you to learn that we are constantly evaluating its use for applications outside our traditional domains. 

Around this proven core tool, we are currently developing a “toolbox” consisting of supplementary and complementary processes, which deal with the selective extraction, crystallization and/or decomposition of metal chlorides. 

In this paper, we shall introduce the building blocks of a metal extraction technology stack based on chloride hydrometallurgy, which we intend to use to develop semi-tailored offerings for miners and metal refiners. While remaining as general as possible, we shall however go into sufficient detail to provide a fair overview on what currently can be achieved in terms of metal separation and extraction in flow sheets, based on a HCl leach. 

Presenting this paper at a Nickel/Cobalt conference, we have included the discussion of a potential HCl-based flow sheet for the extraction of Ni and Co from nickel laterites. 

###### **CHLORIDE HYDROMETALLURGY** 

Chloride hydrometallurgy is not exactly an immensely popular field, neither in a theoretical sense nor when it comes to practical applications. Scientific literature, commercial databases and software tools cover little more than very simple HCl-based systems in any useful depth and range. Among the few industries that have embraced, and widely adopted, chloride hydromet processes are the processors of steel, who use HCl for de-scaling purposes, and the producers of titanium dioxide. 

Despite its inefficiencies and related environmental issues, metal refiners strongly favor the perceived relative simplicity of comparatively dull, but well known and proven, pyrometallurgy over

the promises made by innovative hydrometallurgical flow sheets. 

However, whenever hydrometallurgy has to be chosen over pyrometallurgy (which is typically only the case if smelting is proven to be in no way feasible), sulfuric acid remains the predominant choice for the lixiviant. 

###### **Why is HCl not Commonly used in Hydrometallurgy?** 

There are a couple of strong reasons against the use of HCl in hydrometallurgy, the most obvious being the fact that only a few, highly specialized, successful examples for the metallurgical use of HCl exist, while promoters of sulfuric acid based processes can refer to a great abundance of examples demonstrating the viability of their approach. 

HCl is comparatively volatile and HCl-based processes require close containment. In-situ or heap leaching cannot be performed using hydrochloric acid. Buildings and steel structures near HCl processing facilities face the constant risk of corrosion by condensing hydrochloric acid that has 

439 

found its way into the atmosphere through leakages, scrubber inefficiencies, during maintenance or not-too-uncommon accidents. 

Furthermore, dealing with HCl and metal chloride brines at potentially elevated temperatures requires the skilled use of rather exotic and expensive materials of construction, ranging from thermoplastics such as PP, PVDF, PTFE and PFA, via speciality ceramics and glass linings to alloys of titanium, niobium, and tantalum. Stainless steel is not a technically viable option. 

The number of experienced engineering companies for HCl-based hydrometallurgy is rather small, as is the number of experienced practitioners, who could reliably handle operation and maintenance. Thus, most novel chloride hydromet applications are perceived as rather risky undertakings and HCl is not expected to become anybody’s premier choice anytime soon. 

###### **Why Should its use Still be Considered a Potentially viable Option for Future Refineries?** 

It has been known for many years – and demonstrated at industrial scale – that hydrochloric acid can be regenerated by relatively simple technical means. This sets it apart from most other lixiviants. 

Pyrohydrolysis-based processes, which split metal chlorides into HCl and metal oxides, have been used – predominately in the steel industry<sup>(1)</sup> but also for the production of MgO, NiO, CoO, and Al2O3(2-4). – for more than fifty years. The two most prevalent implementations are the spray roaster process, which yields a fine-grained (mean particle diameter approx. 20 micron) oxide powder with relatively high specific surface, and the fluidized bed process, which produces metal oxide pellets. The Japanese company Chemirite offers a hybrid process, which produces metal oxide powders in an indirectly fired fluidized bed process. 

These processes are limited to rather small treatment capacities per unit and consume a relatively high amount of energy. Thus they are only feasible in a very limited range of applicat

ions or in industrial setups where there is no alternative to HCl as lixiviant, such as the surface treatment of automotive steel before cold rolling. In recent years, however, some companies(5) have worked on a more energy saving process for the recovery of HCl from metal chloride brines. SMS Siemag has recently built the first large scale commercial installation of its “Hydrothermal Acid Regeneration” technology, which regenerates HCl by means of hydrolytic distillation at a fraction of the energy consumption associated with pyrohydrolysis processes. The availability of this new technology, which is a “wet process” and can thus be scaled up to relatively large treatment capacities, renders immediately feasible a variety of HCl-based metal extraction flow sheets, which were disregarded because of poor economics, in the past. ###### **THE SMS SIEMAG CHLORIDE HYDROMET TOOLBOX** SMS Siemag has developed a range of technologies that accomplish the majority of processing steps required for separating mixed metal chlorides efficiently, recover metals as oxides with relatively high purity, and regenerate and purify HCl. ###### **Pyrohydrolysis** Pyrohydrolysis processes (Figure 1) are a class of hydrochloric acid regeneration processes. “Regeneration” means that the vast majority (typically > 99%) of the chlorides contained in the (mixed metal) brines fed to those processes is regained as hydrochloric acid. If metals shall be separated, it is necessary to extract/separate them, e.g. via solvent extraction(6) , before pyrohydrolysis, because they cannot be selectively hydrolyzed. 440 Exhaust Gas

Experiments concerning the selective crystallization of cobalt chloride (CoCl2) and nickel chloride (NiCl2) are conducted. The experimental setup from Figure 9 is used. In order to illustrate the selective precipitation of NiCl2 and CoCl2 from solutions containing FeCl3, CoCl2 and/or NiCl2, concentrations received from ICP and titration are converted into masses by assuming the following: (1) Co and Ni chloride are precipitated as dihydrates (e.g. NiCl2 ⋅ 2 H2O), which accords well with XRD analysis; Fe chloride is precipitated as Fe2Cl6 ⋅ 2 HCl ⋅ 4 H2O<sup>(11)</sup> . (2) the mass of water in the reactor remains constant except the one precipitated as crystal water. Figure 10 to Figure 12 show the masses of dissolved metal chlorides, water, and hydrogen chloride in dependency on the concentration of free hydrogen chloride. Data at a concentration of 0 wt% HCl refer to the masses from Table 2. However, due to the error in analysis, total masses are errorprone as well. 

Increasing amounts of free HCl lead in all experiments to a decrease of dissolved NiCl2 and/or CoCl2 but hardly affect the mass of dissolved FeCl3, which has also been found in the system F

eCl3-H2O-HCl<sup>(11)</sup> : At least at temperatures higher 25°C, the solubility of FeCl3 is independent of the HCl concentration. 

At HCl concentrations higher than 15 to 20 wt% (corresponding to a total chloride concentration of 45 wt%), hardly any NiCl2 remains dissolved in the experiments, Figure 10 and Figure 12. Literature data<sup>(11, 12)</sup> show principally a similar behavior; in any case, the absolute number of free chloride necessary for NiCl2 precipitation in literature and experiments differs, which could be due to both different temperatures and interactions in the multi-electrolyte system. 

CoCl2, Figure 11 and Figure 12, seems to reach a minimum concentration at a free acid concentration between 15 and 20 wt%. For the system CoCl2-HCl-H2O, this minimum can be found as well. Literature data<sup>(11)</sup> reveal that CoCl2 can be salted out with pure FeCl3 concentrations. It appears that FeCl3 concentrations (maximum ca. 25 wt% chloride from FeCl3) in the experiments performed are too low for this effect. Nevertheless, there are many cross-sensitivities in electrolyte systems which cannot be modeled in adequate accuracy. 

In all three experiments, the major metallic elements in the filter cake are Ni or Co (Table 3), which are according to XRD, present as dihydrates (Table 4). ICP analysis and XRD do not find necessarily the same concentrations, as XRD only detects crystalline and known phases. However, there was one phase which could not be detected; it could be Fe2Cl6 ⋅ 2 HCl ⋅ 4 H2O<sup>(11)</sup> but there is no crystallographic data of this compounds available in data bases. Iron chloride is found as ferrous

###### **A PROPOSED FLOW SHEET FOR TREATING NICKEL LATERITES** 

In the following section we will introduce a very general example for a nickel/cobalt extraction process based on the hydrochloric acid leach of an idealized nickel laterite. The proposed flow sheet deliberately ignores certain complications that may aid leaching, such as a secondary leach and any other pre-treatment techniques for ore and brine. For the sake of simplicity and to avoid dealing with unnecessary complexity, we have also eliminated cobalt from the hypothetical feed. 

Based on the experiments performed (see above) we have found some empirical support for the assumptions that: 

- **(a) Nickel and cobalt chloride do not hydrolyze together with ferric iron under certain conditions** 

- **(b) Nickel and cobalt chloride can be crystallized from certain ferric chloride brines by means of increasing free hydrogen chloride concentration in the solution.** 

The proposed flow sheet is based on the hypothesis that (a) and (b) are valid assumptions. 

Studies have yet to be undertaken that will involve the extensive gathering of detailed vapor-liquidequilibrium data for multi component systems including iron, nickel, cobalt, and other metals common in nickel laterite ores. Mechanisms for the inhibition of the formation of elementary chlorine during the hydrolysis of certain metal chlorides in the presence of certain others have to be studied in detail. Means for the suppression of this phenomenon have yet to be developed. 

Based on early experimental data and utilizing the building blocks provided by our “Chloride Hydromet Toolbox” we have developed the idealized flow sheet shown in Figure 13. 

###### **Process Summary** 

The proposed flow sheet assumes a feed containing water, hydrogen chloride, ferric chloride, nickel chloride, and cobalt chloride. It ignores any other impurities and assumes that those have been eliminated in some brine pre-treatment facility or can be separated by extending the flow sheet adequately. The process consumes indirect heat, which can be provided at a low temperature level (<200°C) by means of steam or thermo oil. It requires indirect cooling of some processing stages, preferably by a closed cooling water system or sea water cooling. Its products are: 

- regenerated hydrochloric acid, which is re-used for leaching; 

- a compact, black hematite powder which may be utilized as a relatively pure iron ore substitute in the steel industry; 

- a metal chloride precipitate with a high concentration of nickel and cobalt and relatively low iron and other impurity content, from which the target metals can be conveniently extracted by common techniques such as S/X or I/X. 

Notably, all the components of the proposed flow sheet are made up of processes presented as parts of the “Chloride Hydromet Toolbox”.

**Figure 13: Proposed flow sheet for Hydrochloric Acid Based Nickel Laterite Processing (Omitting Leaching and Brine Conditioning)** 452 ###### **Process Description** As can be seen in the process flow sheet shown in Figure 13, the proposed process consists of ten basic steps. Those shall now be explained individually. - **(1) Preconcentrator.** The preconcentrator is a type of vacuum evaporator. Its purpose is to separate significant quantities of water and free HCl from the feed, thus enabling more energy efficient processing and smaller flow rates (requiring smaller equipment) downstream. By means of vacuum, the boiling point of the brine is lowered to approx. 60 °C. This enables effective heating of the preconcentrator by means of condensation of the super-azeotropic HCl vapor produced in the hydrolyser. The feed itself consists of the leachate as well as the filtrate from the crystallization. Approx. 55% of the liquor fed to the preconcentrator is evaporated. - **(2) Condenser.** The condenser is an indirect heat exchanger, which would typically be fed with cooling water. In the condenser, the vapor from the preconcentrator is condensed. It is operated under the same vacuum conditions as the preconcentrator. The re-condensation of the vapor ensures that the vacuum pumps, which generate the vacuum, do not have to deal with large volume flows and can thus be of conveniently small size. - **(3) Hydrolyser.** Depending on the specific composition of the leachate, it may be required to oxi

dize the liquid leaving the preconcentrator before feeding it to the hydrolyser. It may also be advisable to crystallize undesirable impurities at this stage, but the details of such, rather specific, feed conditioning will not be discussed in any depth in this paper. In the hydrolyser the concentrated liquor is boiled at atmospheric conditions. When designing the example flow sheet a VLE with a boiling point of approx. 184°C was chosen. The operation condition in the hydrolyser depends on the individual metal salt concentrations in the solution and is stabilized by continuous addition of appropriate amounts of water. At this temperature, ferric chloride is decomposed by means of hydrolysis according to the formula 

###### 2 FeCl3 + 3 H2O → Fe2O3 + 6 HCl. 

A vapor consisting of hydrogen chloride and water is boiled off while the crystallized, solid hematite particles are removed via filtration (typically vacuum belt filter or centrifuge). 

Under certain feed conditions it may be necessary to introduce technical means that ensure the efficient oxidation or reduction of certain species. 

- **(4) Recuperator.** The recuperator condenses the vapor from the hydrolyser and heats the preconcentrator at the same time. The vapor from hydrolyser is directly condensed in the recuperator. Boiling point adjustment (as described in the “SMS Siemag Toolbox” chapter) is not required. All the heat of condensation is re-utilized to heat the preconcentrator. 

- **(5) Hematite Filtration.** The filtration of the hematite from the hydrolyser solution is typically facilitated via a vacuum belt filter or a centrifuge with multi stage cake conditioning and cake washing. On the industrial scale, a cake moisture of approx. 10% and a Cl content of less than 0.5% has been obtained. Subsequent caustic washing and drying allow a reduction of the moisture to below 1% and a reduction of the Cl content to below 0.2%. 

- **(6) Filtrate Dilution.** Before sending the clear filtrate to NiCl2 crystallization, its total metal concentration has to be re-adjusted to prevent crystallization of ferric chloride when cooling down the solution. This is done by adding some of the liquid condensed in the condenser. 

- **(7) Crystallization.** The preferred crystallization of NiCl2 is accomplished by sparging the diluted filtrate with hydrogen chloride gas, thus increasing the HCl concentration in the liquid and reducing the solubility of NiCl2. A solid, crystalline product, highly concentrated in NiCl2 can be obtained from this step. This can then be rather conveniently processed into a relatively pure nickel compound by less specific methods, which are beyond the scope of this paper.

-| 455 ###### **ON THE RISK OF INTRODUCING NEW CHLORIDE HYDROMET TECHNOLOGIES** The promises of HCl based flow sheets for the extraction and refining of metals are plentiful. One can rather quickly build process models and obtain proof for some key assumptions with low cost laboratory experiments. Such flow sheets have the potential to provide the nickel/cobalt industry, among others, with extraordinarily cost-efficient, clean processing methods. In some cases this technology is applicable to ore types that have been shunned by those industries so far, because of their incompatibility with the processes virtually dictated by metal extraction orthodoxy. Metal (oxide and concentrate) producers, engineering companies and plant suppliers are typically – and for good and valid reasons – reluctant to introduce new technologies. Historical data show that only a lucky few among the projects implementing breakthrough technologies are completed and commissioned on time and within budget. Even fewer ever reach the planned production capacities and product specifications. Many, however, serve as valuable models and teaching examples for the cautious (but usually much more successful) second-movers, who capitalize on the mistakes made by the pioneers. Processes that depend on the reliable treatment of large quantities of highly corrosive and abrasive liquids at elevated temperatures and pressures – such as chloride hyromet processes – rely on extraordinarily robust and dependable equipment, which not only withstands the often extreme operating conditions but also ensures a high level of safety in case anything goes wrong. When building such facilities, a fair amount of due diligence and upfront analysis is spent on identifying known unknowns and engineering ways to deal with them. Safety margins and fallback scenarios are assumed and inherently safe and dependable solutions are developed. However, besides those known unknowns there are unknown unknowns, i.e. unforeseen difficulties faced during plant start up which might be of a nature that can only be dealt with by spending significant amounts of time

and money. 

We will elaborate in more detail on the common root causes for what materializes as a first-mover disadvantage, link it to our particular experience as a first-mover supplying a chloride hydromet process to a customer in Alabama, USA, and discuss the lessons learned. 

###### **Lack of Data in the Scientific Literature** 

As with any niche technology, reliable data on the chemistry of metals and chlorides is scarce. The very little that is presented by the scientific literature to form the basis for complex modeling software is restricted in temperature, pressure and concentration ranges and deals with very simple systems, typically containing only two or three species. 

Obtaining proprietary data on specific metal chloride systems is a resource-consuming exercise; most people who can afford the required extensive research will be reluctant to share the part of their data that goes beyond trivial findings. 

This makes developing robust HCl-based flow sheets for new applications difficult and expensive. While developing our hydrothermal acid regeneration technology we have done extensive research in collaboration with universities in Europe and Japan to collect reaction and equilibrium data associated with all the processing steps involved. 

###### **Sensitivity to Fluctuations in Feed** 

Even the best model has its limitations. One of the biggest challenges when designing a HCl-based hydromet process is to deal with severe fluctuations in feed, and their consequences for the performance and safety of the process, as well as for the lifetime of the equipment. 

Before building the hydrothermal acid regeneration plant, we built a laboratory-scale mini plant implementing the complete process flow sheet. This plant was run for a period of one year. An extensive amount of data was gathered, and plant behavior under different feed and load scenarios was analyzed in detail. This enabled us to design many features into the industrial plant that had been overlooked, when only relying on theoretical flow sheets and beaker scale tests – especially as some of the least pleasant effects accumulate from minuscule root causes over a long period of time. 

456 

###### **Challenges Associated with Upscaling** 

Large-scale industrial equipment does not always show the behavior one might assume, after linearly extrapolating the performance data measured at a significantly smaller mini plant or pilot plant. 

Thus a representative sized unit of any key component needs to be pre-tested under realistic operating conditions for a prolonged period of time before becoming part of the final design. 

When building the Alabama plant, we bought pumps, valves, sensors, vessels, filters and the like, assembled test setups and operated it with representative process liquors (corrosive, abrasive, hot, contaminated) over prolonged periods of time. This greatly helped to separate the chaff from the wheat and make responsible choices on the kind and manufactur

e of equipment we finally installed. 

There are, however, upscaling risks that cannot be accounted for. One arbitrary example would be the behavior of large-scale crystallizers. Crystallization is in many respects closer to an art than to science and the crystals produced by larger crystallizers – even implementing the same basic parameters such as flow patterns, heat distribution, and retention times – may be different in some of their physical and chemical attributes from what has been produced in smaller devices. 

###### **Challenges Associated with the Required Tight Coupling of Processing Stages** 

The economics of any HCl-based flow sheet depend on the optimized utilization and recuperation of process heat. 

However, process heat can only be recuperated by an upstream processing step, such as vacuum preconcentration, when the downstream step releasing this heat stream is operating at the same time. 

Besides that, the interruption of one downstream process step would require the upstream facilities to either shut down or store their by-products in intermediate storage facilities. This would – given for example the fact that HCl-based flow sheets for Ni/Co would require flow rates of many hundred, or more than one thousand, cubic meters per hour – demand large buffer tank farms. 

Thus, all processing stages have to have an extraordinarily high availability. Redundancy is not a viable option, as (a) the start-up times of redundant processing trains are usually rather long and (b) redundancy would quickly yield unacceptable consequences on the capex. 

Extraordinarily high availability of complex industrial processing arrangements in turn can only be achieved by proven, mature equipment, operated by experienced, well trained and well managed people. 

###### **Challenges associated with Critical Intermediate Products** 

One of the key difficulties with HCl-based flow sheets is that they generate intermediate products with extremely undesirable properties. Some of them are prone to crystallization and thus have to be kept in a heated environment – also during a shut down or after a spillage. Others, such as the liquids involved in crystallization and hydrolysis, contain significant amounts of solids, which, when not continuously agitated, may clog up parts of the plant, calling for major cleaning and maintenance work. 

The absence of such critical intermediate products makes the traditional HCl regeneration technologies so beautifully robust. When a pyrohydrolysis plant is switched off, it is empty. This does not hold true for any wet approach to acid regeneration. Finding sustainable solutions to master the difficulties associated with keeping the relatively large amounts of intermediate products in re-usable conditions, during intended or non-intended plant shutdowns, is at the very top of our research agenda. 

###### **CONCLUSION** 

The introduction of HCl-based flow sheets for the processing of various ores and the energy efficient

extraction of target metals promises dramatic improvements of the economics of certain 

457 

projects – in many cases lending feasibility to the processing of ores that fail to pass any preliminary economic assessment based on more conventional technologies. However, the field requires a significant amount of further study, not only in the laboratories and with software simulation tools, but mainly on the industrial scale, because most crucial success factors are related to the selection of extremely mature, extensively tested, reliable, well-performing and fail-safe equipment. 

Further work will be required to eliminate remaining uncertainties, develop what is now a very young and immature field of technological and industrial interest to a well proven-state of the art level, and make future HCl-based metal extraction facilities and refineries a successful, economically feasible, energy-saving and eco-friendly reality.
